records.title: The role of vagueness in distributive marking: Evidence from Albanian nga
records.abstract: This squib reports a previously undescribed restriction on the Albanian distributive marker nga. While nga combines freely with numeral expressions, speakers judge it strongly degraded with the quantifier shumë ‘many’. An acceptability judgment experiment confirms a selective interaction between distributive marking and quantifier type: the presence of nga lowers acceptability with shumë ‘many’, but not with numerals. Additional judgments suggest that related restrictions may extend to other quantity expressions and to distributive markers in other languages. At the same time, some imprecise numeral expressions appear more acceptable. These findings suggest that distributive marking is not uniformly compatible with all quantity expressions, raising broader questions about how such constructions interact with vagueness.

records.title: Self-destructive feeding as allomorph optimisation
records.abstract: This paper re-examines self-destructive feeding, a type of overapplication opacity, and proposes a new analysis based on the commonalities shared by all attested cases. It is found that all the four cases of self-destructive feeding found in Turkish, Javanese and Japanese involve rules with non-derived environment blocking and attempt to resolve consonant clusters by making changes to the suffix. Based on these common characteristics, a unified analysis is provided to account for not only the self-destructive feeding pattern but also its related phenomena simultaneously, with the help of underspecification and positional/contextual faithfulness under Parallel Optimality Theory. Finally, it is argued that self-destructive feeding is an epiphenomenon of phonologically-conditioned allomorphy.

records.title: Scrambling: Latest Developments and New Challenges
records.abstract: This chapter reviews the relevant literature on scrambling, focusing on three central issues raised by this phenomenon: (i) the relationship between scrambling and free word order—or, framed differently, the base-generation versus movement approaches to scrambling (section 2); (ii) the configurational/positional properties of three distinct scrambling types, namely, VP-internal, clause-internal, and long-distance scrambling (section 3); and (iii) potential triggers for scrambling as a movement operation (section 4). In addition, this chapter addresses ongoing developments in research on scrambling, focusing on how the very option of scrambling is permitted from the perspective of labeling (i.e., Saito 2016, 2018) (section 5). The chapter also explores whether scrambling necessitates movement/Internal Merge, or whether its putative effects can instead be captured through non-movement algorithms such as Minimal Search, following latest extensions of the MP (i.e., Kitahara 2026) (section 6).

records.title: Crossing the external argument in Italian participial and si-passives
records.abstract: This paper addresses the syntactic differences between Italian participial passives (p-pass) and si-passives (s-pass). Both involve a syntactically projected implicit external argument, which licenses depictives and non-logophoric anaphors, but only in p-pass can this argument receive a definite interpretation or alternate with a by-phrase. Furthermore, only the s-pass implicit argument creates intervention effects in the dependency between T and the internal argument. I propose that these differences stem from the fact that the promotion of the internal argument relies on Collins’ (2005) smuggling only in p-pass, and not in s-pass: this can also explain the different availability of inalienable possession readings in the two constructions.

records.title: A principle of balancing non-alternation and alternation in tonal metres
records.abstract: Poetic metres govern the basic rhythmic patterns of verses and lines, and generally require the phonological property they regulate (e.g. stress, weight and/or tone) to alternate within a line to avoid monotony. Using the tonal metre of Middle Chinese regulated verse as an example, this paper proposes that a metre can also require the regulated property not to alternate, and that this requirement is balanced against alternation. The canonical templates of regulated verse require tone categories to alternate within a line, but only to a restricted extent: no non-final syllable in the templates is flanked by two syllables of the opposite category. Beyond the templates, the paper shows in Optimality Theory that the remedies prescribed by traditional prosody for irregular lines follow from the interaction of constraints encoding alternation and non-alternation. The two remedies for guping ‘Lone Even’ (孤平) are outputs of different rankings within a single, partially ranked grammar: the remedy within the line satisfies a non-alternation constraint against a lone Even tone, whereas the remedy in the other line of the couplet satisfies an alternation constraint requiring the two lines of a couplet to be tonal opposites (对). The ‘three-inversion-four-remedy’ pattern (三拗四救) arises when alternation in the cadence of a line takes priority over faithfulness. Finally, I show that this balancing property enriches the typology of poetic metres and parallels restrictions found in the tonal phonology of natural languages, and that metres can be informed by – and thus serve as a window into – natural language phonology.

records.title: Self-destructive feeding and nonderived environment blocking in Parallel OT: an underspecification account
records.abstract: Self-destructive feeding (SDF) is a type of overapplication opacity in which, in rule-based terms, an earlier rule creates the environment for a later rule that in turn removes part of the environment that motivated the earlier one. This paper re-examines four cases of SDF (two in Turkish, one in Javanese and one in Japanese) and shows that they can be accounted for in Parallel Optimality Theory. After introducing the four cases, the paper presents the two properties they share. First, at least one of the processes involved in each interaction is restricted to morpheme junctures and particular morphemes. Second, they resolve consonant sequences at stem-suffix junctures by realising a suffix-initial segment in required contexts. I propose that the alternating segments are underspecified for their association to the skeletal tier, whereas non-alternating segments are fully-specified. In Parallel Optimality Theory, faithfulness to association in general and stronger faithfulness in certain input contexts or positions then account for the lack of morpheme-internal alternations and the SDF outputs in a single input--output evaluation. The three SDF cases involving consonants follow from the rankings needed for the simple alternations alone, and the vowel case requires only one additional ranking. Therefore, SDF involving alternations with zero can be derived in Parallel Optimality Theory once the underlying representations of segments are more appropriately understood.

records.title: THE GRAMMAR OF EVOLUTION IN THE EVOLUTION OF GRAMMARS
keywords: laws of the theory of evolution
records.abstract: Cognitive evolution is to cognitively represented systems what Darwinian evolution is to biological systems. Same problem structure, same solution structure.Therefore, the laws of the theory of evolution (Modern Synthesis and Population Genetics) are the laws of the descent of grammars and their development, as shown in this article.

records.title: What over- and what undergenerates in Right-Node Raising
records.abstract: Belk et al. (2023) and Barros and Vicente (2011) have argued that Right-Node Raising (RNR) requires a dual analysis, as either multidominance or ellipsis. This paper examines RNR at the subword level (e.g., over- and undergenerate) and shows that, like phrasal RNR, subword RNR displays mixed properties diagnostic of both multidominance and ellipsis, supporting a dual analysis at both levels. We argue, however, that the dual approach, as currently implemented, cannot capture certain subword and phrasal RNR data without modification. We therefore propose a modified version of RNR-as-ellipsis, in which focus-marked material can survive ellipsis in situ, and which captures both subword and phrasal RNR, while retaining multidominance as the second component of the dual analysis.

records.title: Modals between control and restructuring: What si makes us see
records.abstract: We investigate the behavior of the Italian verbs ‘must’, ‘can’, and ‘want’, which come in two syntactic guises. Against the view that modals like ‘must’ and ‘can’ are raising verbs, we use evidence from an impersonal construction with the clitic si to argue for an analysis in terms of control and functional restructuring. The proposal allows for a unified syntactic treatment of the three verbs and provides a transparent dissociation of syntactic and semantic properties.

records.title: On Licensing Barest Conditionals: From the Vantage Point of the Syntax-Prosody Interface
records.abstract: This paper investigates two types of barest conditionals in Mandarin, both characterized by their minimal clausal structure and the presence of identical pairing, i.e., two duplicated verbs, such as Gāi chī chī, gāi hē hē ‘Eat when it's time to eat, drink when it's time to drink’, or wh-phrases, like Ài shéi shéi ‘Whoever it may be’ (cf. Tsai 2025). Based on the identical pairing analysis, this paper argues that both types are licensed by an explicit necessity operator, namely the sentence-initial modal: It unselectively binds the pair of identical variables, thereby licensing the donkey-conditional in question (cf. Cheng & Huang 1996, 2020). On the other hand, the type of identical pairing (i.e., verb vs. wh-phrase) depends on which variable acts as the information focus, while the sentence-initial modal serves to license the barest conditional construal. Furthermore, we argue that prosodic fusion, which merges the two separate conditional clauses into a single sentential intonation phrase (cf. Feng 2017), is key to identifying barest conditionals: Only after the fusion do the sentences need to observe the strict requirement of identical pairing. Finally, this paper brings to light the fascinating interaction among register, syntax, and prosody as observed in the formation of barest conditionals.

records.title: Constraints on modal flavor colexification
records.abstract: Modal items are known to often show ambiguity with respect to modal flavor. For example, English 'can' can express both deontic and circumstantial flavor. To date, however, it remains unstudied whether there are particular sets of modal flavors that are more frequently colexified than others across the world’s languages. Here, we avail ourself of the recent database of Uegaki et al. (2024) to uncover natural classes of modal flavor colexification, and to evaluate the degree that these natural classes can be captured using different kinds of ontological structures.

records.title: Patterns of Subordination in Tigrinya
records.abstract: This descriptive chapter provides an overview of the major patterns of subordinate clause formation in Tigrinya, with particular attention to the morphosyntactic markers that introduce relative, adverbial, and complement clauses. Tigrinya employs a small set of clausal prefixes, z(ɨ)-, k(ɨ)-, and kämz(ɨ)-, whose distribution cuts across traditional clause-type distinctions and correlates with syntactic and semantic differences. Relative clauses are formed with z(ɨ)-, which also appears in a range of adverbial and embedded constructions. Complement clauses may be introduced by kämz(ɨ)- or k(ɨ)- triggering in some cases distinct interpretive properties. The chapter situates these patterns within broader discussions of subordination in Ethio-Semitic and Semitic syntax.

records.abstract: This is a brief (informal) reply to Pullum(2026c), which is a review of Postal(2025). records.title: Marginal emphatic consonants in Arabic dialects: Phonemes or not? صوامت التفخيم الثانوية في لهجات العربية: فونيمات أم لا؟
records.abstract: This paper re-examines the status of the so-called “secondary emphatics” in Arabic dialects: consonants traditionally considered to be marginal phonemes with limited emphasis spread effects. These include labial /b, m, f/, coronal /r, l, n/ and velar /k, x/ consonants, among others. An analysis of their phonological behaviour across varieties reveals that only /r/ and /l/ enjoy a phonemic status in certain dialects. The remaining consonants are characterized by a very low functional load, near-exclusive occurrence in loanwords, and strict adjacency to a low vowel, thus casting doubt on their classification as phonemes. An alternative proposal is to treat this behaviour as evidence of a phonemic split in the low vowels, distinguishing front /a/ from a new emphatic vowel /ɑ/. This approach eliminates the need to posit marginal phonemes and generates an economical system, where the new ɑ/ɑ shares a secondary place [dorsal] feature with emphatic consonants.

records.title: Hyperdialectalism and de-opacization in Camuno vowel harmony
records.abstract: Camuno is a dialect of Eastern Lombard characterized by stress-driven high vowel harmony where all mid vowels preceding stressed [i] and round ones preceding stressed [u] rise. The low central [a] does not participate in the harmony and is opaque, that is, preceding vowels also do not participate in the harmony. However, a pattern of transparency of [a] is attested in the language. In this pilot study, I investigate the possible correlation between perceived fluency and acceptability of transparent [a] in Camuno. The results reveal a clear tendency to (perceptual) hyper-dialectalism by younger and less fluent speakers, which I argue to be motivated by the specificities of the sociolinguistic context where Camuno is spoken. In addition to describing an emerging pattern of micro-variation, the results open questions about the role of hyper-dialectalism as a driving force for language change in the context of dilalia (Berruto, 1987). [This is an initial pilot study, comments and suggestions are very welcome]

records.title: A PredP Analysis of English Resultative Constructions:Focusing on the Asymmetry of Wh-Extraction
records.abstract: This paper proposes a novel syntactic analysis of English resultative constructions within the framework of modern Minimalist syntax (Chomsky 2024; Kitahara and Seely 2025). Challenging traditional Small Clause analyses, we argue that the result predicate is accommodated within a functional phrase, PredP (Bowers 1993), separating the state-holder from the main verb's direct object position. Combined with the FormCopy operation and Minimal Search, our model accounts for the long-standing WH-extraction asymmetry between paint-type and consider-type resultatives. Specifically, we demonstrate that consider-type verbs lack a lexical object position (DP2), preventing FormCopy from generating the required search path for WH-extraction. This structural difference naturally derives the extraction restriction without positing ad-hoc constraints, offering a unified account of syntactic relations and semantic interpretations in resultative constructions.

records.title: R in the Tigris qeltu-dialects of Mesopotamia
records.abstract: The Tigris qeltu-dialects are known to have a uvular fricative ġ in place of historical rāʔ, but existing side by side with a tapped r, and their occurrence is both phonologically and sociolinguistically conditioned. This chapter first outlines the sociolinguistic variation, but then concentrates on the phonological behavior of (inclusive) R in three dialects of this qeltu subgroup, namely, Maṣlāwi Arabic and Christian and Jewish Baghdadi Arabic, based on data collected from four native informants via two reading tasks. The objective is to examine the lexical categories, distributional patterns, and possible phonological processes in which R participates, such as loan vs. native words, minimal pairs, cooccurrence restrictions on consonant combinations, and various types of assimilation. Although the data exhibit discrepancies between the dialects, evidence confirms the existence of two R phonemes in all three of them: a dorsal fricative /ġ/ which is a reflex of old rāʔ merged with inherited ġayn, and a coronal sonorant /r/ found mainly in loanwords and some native words with specifiable phonological contexts. A representational analysis, formulated in the framework of feature geometry, demonstrates that /r/ is exclusively rhotic while /ġ/ is not.

records.title: Statistical Evidence for an Upper Palaeolithic Proto-writing System in Bacon et al. 2023: A Response to Critiques
records.abstract: Bacon et al. 2023 argue that Upper Palaeolithic mark sequences track the seasonal timing of animal reproductive cycles and so represent the earliest evidence for the use of an abstract notation system representing information, at least twenty-six thousand years ago, over twenty thousand years before the earliest Sumerian writing system. This paper evaluates the validity of those claims by subjecting the original dataset to rigorous statistical re-analyses. It addresses the methodological critiques raised in subsequent literature by i) clarifying the original species-level statistical analysis, ii) reporting previously omitted right-to-left sign positional data, iii) discussing the most appropriate unit of analysis to be employed in statistical tests of this data, iv) explaining that the baseline probabilities of finding matches to birth or mating are known and differ between species, and v) presenting new sets of analyses using Poisson-Binomial tests and Monte-Carlo permutation tests both of which can take account of these issues. In addition, we rectify figure-generation alignment errors erroneously introduced in our original paper. Strong statistical associations persist between non- sequence lengths and mating periods, and between sign variables and birth windows. The principal quantitative findings of Bacon et al. thus remain robust.

records.title: The semantics of prohibition: Normative authority and deontic modality in Mandarin jìnzhǐ
records.abstract: Existing approaches to deontic modality, directives, and social relations provide important resources for analyzing prohibition, but a compositional question remains: how does a lexical prohibition report relate an actual normative eventuality to an intensional target and to the authority of its source? Focusing on Mandarin jìnzhǐ `prohibit', we develop an event-based deontic semantics that distinguishes the norm-bearing eventuality from the possible target event and uses source--addressee jurisdiction to constrain the selection of negative requirements. The resulting analysis derives an event-relative deontic obligation without entailing either compliance or violation in the actual world. It also distinguishes normative addressees from embedded thematic agents, accommodating both interpersonal prohibitions and institutional restrictions on non-agentive eventualities. We thus show how event relativity and socially grounded authority jointly contribute to the lexical semantics of prohibition.

records.title: The Morphosyntactic–Semantic Unity of the Early Middle Japanese Realis Form Izenkei: the -ru ≈ -re allomorphy and the so-called kakari-musubi
records.abstract: This study proposes a unified morphosyntactic–semantic account of the suffixal form -re found in the EMJ realis paradigm — the so-called izenkei — and related phenomena. It argues that -re is a contextual allomorph of the inflexional suffix -ru, which marks a clause as [0PAST, +ACTUAL-WORLD-COMMITMENT] and thereby presents the eventuality expressed by that clause as belonging to the actual world lato sensu. It surfaces as -re when the clause is set as a premise. This premise-setting environment is supplied overtly by the suffixes -ba [+CONDITIONAL] and -do(mo) [+CONCESSIVE], and covertly by the phonologically null suffix -Ø [+PREM(ISE-SETTING)] in the =koso type of kakari-musubi. Thus, the focus particle =koso does not itself condition the allomorphy -ru → -re, but merely focalises a constituent not containing the finite predicate within a clause already set as a premise by -Ø [+PREM]. In the =zo/=namu type, by contrast, a clause with a topic–comment articulation is first constructed, and its topic constituent containing the finite predicate is nominalised by -Ø [+NOM(INAL)] so that it can be treated as a topic NP. The focus particle =zo or =namu is then added to the comment. The resulting construction is analysed as a COPULA-LESS INVERTED PSEUDO-CLEFT in which the comment/focus precedes the nominalised topic/background without the intervention of the pseudo-copula =n-ari. This pseudo-cleft has two further types: the =ka type and the =ya type. The distribution of the focus particles is simple: in an interrogative clause, =ka is selected if an interrogative phrase constitutes the focus, whereas =ya is selected if a non-interrogative phrase constitutes the focus; in a declarative clause, =zo/=namu is selected. Cross-linguistically, Spanish and Portuguese provide close structural parallels to the =zo/=namu, =ya and =ka types. The =koso type, by contrast, contains no such nominalised topic phrase containing a finite predicate and is therefore NOT a PSEUDO-CLEFT. NOR does there seem to be any syntactic evidence that it is an IT-CLEFT. Finally, the absence of a special predicate form with the focus particles =ha and =mo follows from the set-based nature of their focalisation, which presupposes a contextually relevant set rather than a clause set as a premise by -Ø [+PREM]. Furthermore, in these constructions, no constituent containing a finite predicate constitutes the topic, and hence no such constituent is nominalised by -Ø [+NOM] to form a topic NP. Accordingly, the particles themselves do not determine the predicate forms. Rather, the configuration is constructed FIRST and only THEN determines both the predicate form and which focus particle may occur. Traditional particle–predicate concord called kakari-musubi is therefore reanalysed as a surface correspondence between two consequences of the same independently constructed structure.

records.title: Pathways to pied-piping with inversion: the view from Sm’algyax
records.abstract: This paper explores the possible derivational pathways to the phenomenon known as pied-piping with inversion (PPwI), through the lens of possessor extraction in Sm’algyax (Tsimshianic; British Columbia/Alaska). I first consider two derivational pathways that differ in how the wh-word comes to precede the possessed noun, and more generally, how the wh-possessive constituent comes to occupy clause-initial position. In the standard “inversion” analysis (e.g., Aissen 1996; Coon 2009), these properties are derived through two steps of Ā-movement. In the “no inversion” analysis (Royer et al. 2026), they arise from the base-generation of a wh-word in the form of a non-verbal predicate together with operator movement inside the wh-predicate’s clausal complement. I argue that although Sm’algyax independently permits both wh-movement and wh-predication, possessor extraction nevertheless requires an inversion step. I then show that such configurations are compatible with a base-generated wh-predicate analysis.

records.title: Ibero-Romance prepositional infinitives: Microvariation and Exceptional Case-Marking
records.abstract: Although prepositional infinitives (PIs) are generally rare in Spanish as these are selected mainly by reflexive verbs and non-reflexive verbs tend to select the bare infinitive in accordance with verbal argument structure (Green (1988:109-110), Subirats-Rüggeberg (1987:4ff)), PIs headed by de are attested as complements of non-reflexive verbs in Spanish dialects in parallel to other Romance varieties. This phenomenon known as el deísmo displays microvariation between peninsular and Latin American varieties (Castillo-Ros (2017a)): in the former (Andalucía, La Mancha) de-infinitives are selected in a range of constructions that have parallels in other Romance languages and older stages of Spanish (Di Tullio (2011, 2013), Camus Bergareche (2013), Benito and Pato (2015)), whereas in the latter (grammatical for speakers from Perú and Ecuador, acceptable for speakers from Chile and Venezuela) de-infinitives are used only in the passive of Exceptional Case-Marking (ECM) constructions and not in the active (Montalbetti (1999)), which suggests that el deísmo can be parameterised between peninsular and Latin American Spanish in terms of grammatical voice (active and passive respectively). While the historical-comparative distribution of de-infinitives suggests that these PIs stem from proto-Romance/Latin, especially Latin prepositional gerund(ive)s which suppletively represent the oblique relations of the infinitive and are collocated with the relevant lexical verbs (Vincent (1988:68-70, 1999:4-6), Schulte (2007:79, 87-90, 106-109)), the retention of de in the passivisation of Latin American ECM-constructions is striking evidence that de is essential for ECM A(rgument)-raising (cf Castillo Ros (2017b)), which is traditionally formalised as the raising of the subject of the embedded infinitive to the matrix subject position via a matrix object-position (Lasnik (1999, 2001)). In a Phase-theoretic approach (Chomsky (2000, 2001)) where Phase-Impenetrability Condition (PIC) makes it necessary for the raised argument to be visible to the matrix verb (Sheehan and Cyrino (2018)), this is possible only if the infinitival complement projects an extra projection (i.e. not bare infinitive) as is attested cross-linguistically (Borgonovo (1996), Felser (1998, 1999), Hornstein, Nunes and Martins (2008)), which can be determined to be de (Fin(ite)/M(ood)) (cf Rizzi (1997)). In this framework, it is possible to parameterise el deísmo in terms of two structural positions: SpecFin/M and SpecAppl(icative), both of which are essential for the passivisation and A-raising in ECM-constructions. While de (M) provides an escape-hatch (SpecFin/M) for the embedded subject to move to the matrix clause, it can be argued that peninsular Spanish varieties do not project ApplP while Latin American ones do, which can explain why passivisation of ECM verbs is possible in the latter and not in the former. Moreover, in this derivational model where the infinitive needs to be ‘big’ in order to facilitate A-raising of the embedded subject, the Spanish infinitive seems to be relatively ‘small’ in contrast to other Romance languages (e.g. Italian where the bare infinitive permits ECM A-raising) as an overt complementizer (de) is required to allow A-raising of the embedded subject to the matrix clause (Sheehan (2023)).

records.title: An ex-situ focus semantics
records.abstract: Focus semantics is intimately linked with question semantics, but syntactically the two phenomena come apart in English and other European languages: while at least one wh-phrase in questions must move to an ex-situ, sentence-initial position, foci generally remain in situ. This has led to two different accounts being widely adopted for focus and question semantics: on the one hand, an in-situ semantics for focus that assigns a set meaning for the focussed constituent and point-wise composition projects the set meaning to higher phrasal constituents; on the other hand, an ex-situ semantics for questions that assumes movement of wh-phrases above a question complementizer that takes a propositional argument to describe a set of propositions. Though it is well known that an in-situ semantics like that for focus can also be provided for questions—in fact, the alternative semantics for questions is even older than the alternative semantics for focus (Hamblin, 1973)—the opposite is not widely known: an ex-situ semantics for focus like the standard semantics for questions. This type of semantics is presented below.

records.title: Marathi polar question particles and (non-)canonicity of questions
records.abstract: In this paper, I describe syntax and semantics of Marathi polar questions and polar questions particles to place them on the broader Indo-Aryan landscape. In doing so, I argue that Marathi polar question particles uniformly signal information-seeking polar questions when clause-final, while their clause-medial occurrences – wherever grammatical – signal non-canonical questions of various kinds. I show that this indicates a strict mapping between the syntactic and semantic-pragmatic notions of canonicity of questions and necessitates a closer examination of semantic-pragmatic properties of clause-medial polar question particles from Indo-Aryan languages previously described in the literature.

records.title: The Direction of Disagreement: What Departures from the Majority Term Teach a Text-Only Learner
records.abstract: Speakers of the same language draw category boundaries in slightly different places. A color chip that most speakers call green may therefore be called blue by others. Disagreement of this kind is usually treated as noise: typological mode maps retain only each chip's majority term, and labeling pipelines combine annotations by majority vote. Disagreement also carries a cost for communication, but for a learner who has access only to names, the direction of disagreement records which categories are neighbors. Departures from the majority happen mostly near boundaries and almost always use the term for the category on the other side. A simple model compares this evidence with the cost to a listener: as the spread of boundaries decreases, the listener's extra error decreases quadratically, while the learner's evidence about neighboring categories decreases only linearly. We test this account with small language models trained only on object-naming sentences. In an artificial language with a known scale, their object representations reflect the scale only when speakers' boundaries differ. In 92 languages of the World Color Survey, randomly replacing the minority terms while preserving where and how often departures occur reduces the recoverable color geometry in every language for the naming text and in 90–92 languages for the models. Retaining only the majority term removes this geometry.

records.title: Hallucination, Formal Reasoning, and the α-Gradient: A Linguistic Framework for AI Architecture
records.abstract: This paper applies the gradient conventionalization framework developed in Mozahid (2025a, 2025b, 2026) to the architecture of artificial intelligence systems, arguing that the persistent divide between statistical and categorical AI is fundamentally a semantic phenomenon rather than an engineering one. The framework operationalizes meaning components through levels of intersubjective agreement (α), providing a principled account of why different AI architectures can process only certain ranges of the α-gradient. Categorical systems operate exclusively at α→1.0; large language models (LLMs) operate across α=0.30–0.95, most reliably in the α=0.70–0.90 zone of default entailment. α-level assignments are derived from corpus-distributional measures established independently in Mozahid (2025a), treating AI behavioral data as a convergent test rather than the source of those assignments — a methodological structure that resolves a potential circularity and transforms divergences between predicted and observed AI behavior into theoretically informative evidence. The architectural mapping yields four contributions: it reframes LLM hallucination as α-level misassignment, the structural mismatch between assertoric output form and probabilistic generative mechanism; it reframes neuro-symbolic hybrid systems as implicitly α-stratified architectures whose routing criterion should be α-level rather than domain or task type; it argues that formal systems are natural language driven to α→1.0 through definitional stipulation, connecting the framework to debates in the philosophy of mathematics; and it identifies α-elevation — conventionalization's upward pressure on intersubjective agreement — as a theoretical concept currently absent from AI architecture research but necessary for any principled account of how formal reasoning emerges from natural language processing.

records.title: Beyond Semantic Prosody: Reassessing the Directionality of Connotative Meaning in Lexical Semantics
records.abstract: The theory of semantic prosody posits that words acquire evaluative coloring through repeated collocation with positively or negatively charged contexts. While this usage-based framework effectively describes distributional patterns, it faces persistent theoretical challenges regarding directionality: does usage shape meaning, or does meaning shape usage? This paper demonstrates that for a significant class of frequently studied words, inherent lexical-semantic profiles act as primary filters that attract words to congruent discourse contexts, with collocational patterns emerging as consequences rather than causes of connotative meaning. Through systematic analysis of cause, utterly, commit, set in, foster, and regime, integrating published corpus analyses with theoretical linguistics, this study shows that their attested collocational skews reflect underlying semantic features—agentive, intensive, volitionally binding, gradual-onset, facilitative, and system-control profiles, respectively. Counterevidence from neutral and positive contexts in multiple corpora undermines claims of fixed evaluative prosodies while supporting profile-based explanations. Diachronic evidence demonstrates that semantic profiles remain stable across centuries even as specific collocational patterns vary, supporting the claim that profiles drive usage rather than absorbing evaluative charge from it. This reconceptualization addresses the problematic lexical-encyclopedic dichotomy, demonstrating through evidence from large language models, language testing, and cross-linguistic research that the traditional boundary between lexical meaning and world knowledge is far more permeable than conventional accounts acknowledge. The findings have practical implications for lexicography, natural language processing, and language pedagogy.

records.title: Profiles, Not Prosodies: A Weighted-Feature Diagnostic for Connotative Meaning in Lexical Semantics
records.abstract: The theory of semantic prosody holds that words acquire evaluative coloring through repeated collocation with charged contexts, such that connotation is absorbed from usage rather than encoded in the lexicon. This paper argues that the phenomena motivating that theory are real but have been correctly measured and incorrectly attributed. It treats lexical meaning as a weighted bundle of semantic features and distinguishes two independent readouts of that bundle: a structural axis, tracking coverage of a word's non-evaluative content, and a valence axis, tracking its evaluative content specifically. The prosody tradition has read collocational skew almost exclusively onto the valence axis; this paper argues that for a substantial class of frequently studied words the skew belongs on the structural axis instead, and that this misattribution, not any failure to detect real pattern, is the source of the tradition's most persistent unsolved problems. Through analysis of cause, utterly, commit, set in, foster, and regime, alongside the contrasting case of murder, the paper develops a falsification procedure — the contradiction test — for locating a feature's conventionalization: features admitting structured, unmarked counterexamples are diagnosed as weak; those admitting none, as strong. The six classical words encode strongly conventionalized structural profiles alongside weak valence content, while murder's valence sits strong, fused with its descriptive content. The account answers two problems named in the prosody literature — the introspection problem and the causal-direction problem — and distinguishes its diagnostic claim from gradient absorption accounts, which tolerate exceptions but lack a mechanism for locating them.

records.title: Knowledge as Conventionalized Arbitrary Relations: Toward a Theory of Epistemology
records.abstract: This paper proposes that encyclopedic knowledge — what we know about the world, as distinct from what follows from definitions or logical structure — consists fundamentally of conventionalized arbitrary relations. Drawing on Saussurean sign-arbitrariness, Kripkean modal semantics, and the gradient conventionalization framework developed in prior work on lexical meaning, the paper argues that every empirical claim depends on a contingent carving of reality into concepts and a contingent act of reference-fixing that anchors those concepts to worldly entities. Both operations are arbitrary in the Saussurean sense and require intersubjective stabilization before they can function as publicly warranted knowledge rather than as private epistemic state. The thesis is tested against apparent counterexamples — Kripke's necessary a posteriori, scientific laws, mathematical truths, and perceptual beliefs — each reducing to either a system-internal relation or a conventionalized arbitrary relation not necessary in any world-independent sense. The degree to which a claim qualifies as publicly warranted knowledge corresponds to its degree of conventionalization within a specified epistemic community, operationalized through the alpha coefficient developed in prior work. The framework remains agnostic about inaccessible first-person standpoints, a stance illustrated through wrongly convicted defendants, deceased persons, and the Cartesian cogito. Philosophy, on the resulting picture, is not a producer of α-scorable knowledge but the generative substrate through which the conceptual carvings over which conventionalization operates are invented, contested, and revised.

records.title: Gradient Conventionalization: A Unified Framework for Lexical Semantics and Social Epistemology
records.abstract: This paper proposes a unified framework that reconceives the relationship between lexical meaning and world knowledge as a gradient of conventionalization rather than a categorical distinction. Meaning components are distinguished by their level of conventionalization, operationalized as degree of speaker agreement, rather than by membership in "lexical" versus "encyclopedic" categories. The framework introduces a five-level gradient — reference, denotation, sense, cultural connotation, private connotation — corresponding to decreasing intersubjective agreement, and a typology of entailments (strong, default, weak) correlated with these levels. This reconceptualization clarifies semantic prosody, explains why some arguments converge while others polarize, and connects lexical semantics to social epistemology. Central to the epistemological application is the diagnosis of alpha misattribution: the error of treating a term whose meaning is genuinely low-agreement as though it carried the stability of a high-agreement term, an error that converts unresolved conceptual disagreement into the appearance of bad-faith resistance to consensus. The framework generates testable predictions about semantic change, argument dynamics, and the conditions under which making agreement levels explicit can reduce polarization.

records.title: A Gradient Framework for Connotative Meaning: Weak Entailments and Conventionalization
records.abstract: This paper challenges the traditional lexical-encyclopedic dichotomy in formal semantics by proposing that linguistic meaning and world-knowledge exist on a gradient of conventionalization rather than forming categorically distinct types of knowledge. Through an analysis of entailment strength and intersubjective agreement patterns, I argue that the field's persistent failure to theorize connotative meaning stems from systematically conflating two distinct phenomena: cultural connotation (systematic, community-level patterns that generate weak entailments) and private connotation (idiosyncratic, individual associations). Drawing on evidence from semantic prosody research, arbitrariness of the linguistic sign, language acquisition patterns, and computational modeling, I develop a gradient framework in which meaning components are distinguished by their level of conventionalization rather than by categorical membership in "denotative" versus "connotative". This reconceptualization provides theoretical tools for understanding how lexical semantic profiles generate systematic distributional patterns while remaining resistant to conscious introspection, thereby resolving longstanding puzzles in the relationship between word meaning and usage patterns.

records.title: Varieties of headless relative clauses in Tigrinya
records.abstract: This paper presents the first systematic description of headless relative clauses in Tigrinya (Semitic; Eritrea and Ethiopia; SOV). Drawing on novel fieldwork data, it examines three types of headless relatives, namely light-headed, super-free, and free-choice relatives. The data show that, unlike many other languages, Tigrinya forms both headed and headless relative clauses using the same morphosyntactic strategy, which involves the relativizer z(ɨ)- without overt wh-elements. Headless relatives in Tigrinya do not rely on interrogative wh-structures, in contrast to languages such as English. Notably, free relatives are not attested. Instead, all headless relative clauses share a structural core with headed relatives, differing only in the presence or absence of nominal and determiner layers. By documenting this pattern, the paper identifies a previously underdescribed strategy in Afro-Asiatic. These findings refine the typology of relativization, provide empirical evidence for cross-linguistic variation in relative clause formation, and establish a foundation for formal analyses of Tigrinya and related languages.

It conforms to universal and cross-linguistic trends of markedness (Aissen (2003), Serzant and Witzlack (2018)), namely nominal animacy and referentiality (Kliffer (1995)), verbal affectedness and transitivity (Kaiser and von Heusinger (2007)), and clausal topicality (Leonetti (2004)), which, in formal cartographic terms (Cinque (1999, 2002)), correspond to different features in the nominal, verbal and clausal domains, namely [+human/animate] in the nominal lexical head (N), functional projections of referentiality denoting definiteness (D), specificity ([+specific]), and Phi-features of Person (Pers) and Number (Num), verbal projections of agentivity (DO) and kinesis (BECOME) (InitiateP and ProcessP/ResultP respectively in Folli (2002), Ramchand (2008)), and topic in the left-periphery (TopicP). It is hence possible to account for the selection of ad as a Case-marker ([i-K]) (Giusti (1996)) by positing selectional features ([u-K]) on the various projections above. records.title: What Prepositional Object Gaps Tell Us about Merge and Linearization
The curious case of the two-headed phrase: The symmetrical syntax of co-compounds
records.abstract: Co-compounds (CC) are pairs of morphosyntactically parallel and semantically related elements that constitute a single morphosyntactic and semantic unit. Usually described as a type of (asyndetic) coordination in the typological literature, they have only received sporadic attention from generative syntacticians, and have mostly been analysed as a subtype of exocentric compounds (Scalise, Fábregas & Forza 2009). In contrast to this previous analysis, based on data from two Uralic languages (Hungarian and Surgut Khanty), we argue that co-compounding is a syntactic operation: an instance of two heads undergoing Merge and being dominated by a shared layer of functional projections. While an implicit assumption of endocentricity (Chomsky 1970) and the projection principle (Chomsky 1993) has been that it is exactly one head that heads and projects a phrase, we argue that as long as a few conditions (that CCs are subject to) are met, the existence of such two-headed phrases is unproblematic for the standard understanding of these two core concepts. We also address the issue of labelling that emerges when two heads undergo Merge in a symmetric fashion. We model the semantics of CCs in terms of substitution by a shared superordinate term plus universal or existential closure. We also address variation between Hungarian and Surgut Khanty in terms of (i) the required degree of semantic relatedness between the two elements and (ii) the availability of dual/plural marking and a conjunctive interpretation; we relate this variation to the very different functional load that co-compounding carries in the two languages.

records.title: Dr.
records.abstract: This study explores how various discourse structures influence the identity formation of non-native speakers as ESL learners and teachers within a specified time and space. Discourse is understood as an organizing and coherent system of knowledge expressed through linguistic means and praxis (Pavlenko, 2003). It embodies particular perspectives and encompasses the ways of associating in which tools, thoughts, words, values, and objects are associated and systematized in specific times and spaces for the purpose of constructing and recognizing and identities and practices. The study is based on a real-life account of a multilingual student proficient in several languages such as English, Sindhi, Urdu, Siraiki, Punjabi, and Hindi. The essay examines the role and significance of both dominant and alternative discourses in shaping the learner’s identity throughout her experiences of learning and teaching English in her native country. Four discourses are discussed: the discourse of native speakers and Standard English, the non-native speaker or L2 learner identity, the appropriation of a multilingual identity, and the discourse of classroom interaction. These discourses frame the ways individuals think about the experience particular practices and phenomena; they have historically dominated English educational contexts and have shaped—and reshaped—learner identity over time. The findings support Cook’s (1999) concept of multicompetence, which envisions an imagined community for multilinguals and positions second language learners as empowered and legitimate users of the target language. In light of these findings, translanguaging pedagogy is recommended as an effective approach for adapting instructional practices within multilingual contexts

records.title: Non-canonical agreement in predicational copular clauses: Evidence from Polish
records.abstract: This paper examines several understudied and unusual types of copular constructions in Polish, in which the copula agrees with the predicate rather than the subject. It argues that this seemingly unexpected agreement pattern follows from a well-known principle: the controller of agreement is the highest accessible phrase in the domain of agreement. This conclusion is defended against appearances, which suggest that the controller of agreement is not the highest accessible phrase in the constructions at hand. In the process, the paper advances several theoretical claims, including the proposal that the demonstrative found in the subject position in such constructions is structurally reduced and lacks a case projection, that certain non-agreeing leftmost phrases are base-generated above TP, and that there are two flavours of Pred in Polish, including a highly defective Pred which combines with nominal predicates in the nominative instead of the usual instrumental of predication. The paper also reports the discovery of long-distance agreement in Polish, apparently not noted so far in the context of Slavic.

records.title: Finding Worlds to Believe in - Natural Language Semantics and the Axiom of Choice
records.abstract: This paper shows that within possible world semantics (PWS), any principled attempt to identify the common content of two beliefs based on notions such as subject-matter or maximal informativeness ultimately requires an appeal to the Axiom of Choice (AC). While PWS can plausibly assume that shared content exists, it cannot construct it. We contrast this with truthmaker semantics (TMS), where common content can instead be explicitly constructed from the truthmakers of the input propositions, via two independently motivated and equivalent constructions, without invoking AC. We take this to argue that axiomatic parsimony, e.g., whether a framework must assume the existence of certain entities rather than construct them, constitutes a novel dimension along which semantic theories can be compared, and suggest that this difference may be linked to whether a framework's basic entities carry mereological structure.

records.title: Test
Invisible inanimates and the syntax of pronominal prefixes in Northern Iroquoian
records.abstract: Northern Iroquoian languages are famous for the complexities of their agreement systems, realized through three sets of ‘pronominal prefixes’. Drawing on new and existing material from Kanien’kéha (Mohawk), this article proposes a formal model that captures the range of empirical patterns using standard assumptions about argument structure and agreement, combined with the proposal that inanimate nominals have no person, number, or gender (φ) features and are thus invisible to the agreement system. This result is important in light of the fact that Kanien’kéha and its close relative Oneida have been the subject of proposals for major parametric variation among human languages. In The polysynthesis parameter, Baker (1996) draws primarily on Kanien’kéha, arguing that a macroparameter relating to the realization of agreement morphology is responsible for a range of morphosyntactic phenomena in Kanien’kéha and other polysynthetic languages. Koenig and Michelson (2015) examine agreement puzzles in Oneida and argue for a different type of macroparameter: that Northern Iroquoian languages differ from other languages in lacking a level of argument structure and local syntactic selection altogether. In this article, I argue that the core empirical patterns can be captured through the proposal that inanimate nominals are featureless, and that reference to hierarchical structure is necessary to capture the full range of facts. The absence of φ-features on inanimates in turn has implications both for the typology of nominal features and for the Polysynthesis Parameter, a parameter that requires all arguments in polysynthetic languages to be morphologically referenced on the verb.

records.title: Laryngeal reduction and mora deletion in Mixtec: Phonetics in phonology
records.abstract: This paper describes a process of laryngeal reduction in San Martín Peras Mixtec (SMPM; ISO: jmx), an Otomanguean language spoken in Oaxaca and by diasporic communities throughout Mexico and the US. In this process, roots containing a laryngealized vowel often appear in a highly reduced form in fast speech. Laryngeal reduction is gradient, dependent on speech rate, and lacks a phonologically defined conditioning environment, giving it the characteristics of a phonetic process. However, it is at least sometimes correlated with a phonological process of mora deletion, as evidenced by the fact that some highly reduced laryngealized roots—but no unreduced laryngealized roots—undergo a phonological tone sandhi alternation that applies only to mono-moraic rising tones. The phonological process of mora deletion is argued to be conditioned by the same phonetic factors that drive laryngeal reduction, constituting an instance of a phonological process triggered by purportedly phonetic factors.

records.title: Fonology: Phonological analysis in R
records.abstract: Fonology is an R package for phonological analysis, with tools for grapheme-to-phoneme conversion, syllabification, stress assignment, sonority-based measures, natural-class feature matrices, and maximum entropy modeling. It provides primary support for Portuguese, Spanish, French, and Italian, and English transcription that allows user-correctable overrides and heuristic fallback for out-of-vocabulary forms. Accuracy of grapheme-phoneme conversion ranges from 94% to 99% (using a combination of lookup and regex). Functions are vectorized, which yields fast performance over large texts (fast for R, that is). The package is designed to support reproducible phonological research and teaching by integrating common analytical workflows into a consistent R interface, including transcription, feature-based generalization, quantitative phonotactic measures, and visualization-ready outputs.

records.title: phonokit: a toolkit to create phonological representations in Typst
records.abstract: Creating high-quality phonological representations in academic documents is often time-consuming and requires juggling multiple tools and LaTeX packages (most notably TikZ). This vignette introduces phonokit, an open-source Typst package designed to streamline the creation of phonological structures while maintaining typographical precision. The package provides intuitive functions for IPA transcription (supporting tipa input conventions), IPA vowel charts and consonant tables with built-in language inventories and flexible arrows, prosodic representations (syllables, feet, prosodic words, metrical grids), sonority profiles, autosegmental phonology (feature spreading, tone, delinking), multi-tier representations for complex non-linear structures such as Government Phonology and CV phonology, feature geometry, SPE feature matrices, Optimality Theory tableaux, Harmonic Grammar, Noisy Harmonic Grammar, Maximum Entropy grammars, and Hasse diagrams for constraint rankings. All functions prioritize minimal input syntax while automatically handling complex typographical challenges such as dynamic spacing, line crossing prevention, and proper alignment. phonokit aims to reduce cognitive load in document preparation, allowing phonologists to focus on content rather than formatting. The package is freely available through Typst's package repository and is under active development.

records.title: Tone after phonologization: The diachronic filter and the representation of laryngeal categories
records.abstract: The posture of the larynx modulates fundamental frequency mechanically, and this linkage underlies a robust typological association between voicing, pitch, and phonation across the world’s languages. A long tradition of phonological theory explains the association by encoding laryngeal substance in tonal features. This article argues that the explanation fails. One laryngeal source is phonologized as categorically distinct objects, as tone, voice register, ballistic stress, or phrasal melody, varying language by language. Once phonologized, tonal categories can detach from their phonetic origins, patterning as abstract classes rather than according to their phonetic correlates. The association be- tween voice and tone is not a matter of representational content; it is explained by diachrony, in the mechanics of the larynx and the channel of transmission through which sound systems pass during acquisition. Phonological representations are most adequately viewed as abstract, substance-free, emergent, and language-specific, relieved of an explanatory burden they cannot meet.

records.title: The Unbearable Simplicity of Being Something
records.abstract: This paper investigates a correlation between copula agreement and anaphoric potential in Czech and German copular clauses. We argue that this correlation stems from a structural ambiguity between standard predicational clauses and a novel category of classificatory clauses. To capture the intuition that nominal predicates in the latter act as classifiers rather than simple property-denoting expressions, we introduce Locus Semantics. By distinguishing between an entity and its mental representation (locus), this framework allows for a formal treatment of grammatical features as class-presuppositions. We propose that while predicational structures resolve conflicting class-presuppositions via a type-shifter—allowing only for accommodated anaphora—classificatory structures utilize a silent, mediating pronoun. This pronoun introduces a distinct locus, thereby licensing non-canonical agreement and direct discourse anaphora.

records.title: Topic pronouns in Czech: Argument drop in disguise
records.abstract: Czech, the West Slavic language at the centre of our investigation, employs two varieties of stand-alone demonstratives. The first type is an agreeing demonstrative ten/ta/to…‘this.m.sg/f.sg/n.sg’ that agrees with 𝜙-features of its antecedent, whenever these are available. This standalone demonstrative is strictly referential, and in general displays common cross-linguistic behaviour. 1 Our focus will be on the other type: the non-agreeing variant, which we dub to, based on its Nominative form. This stand-alone demonstrative is always realized as neuter singular, irrespective of the gender and number of its antecedent. Previous literature has characterized to as the Czech equivalent of English it, either as a ‘nonperson’ pronoun (Hlavsa 1975, building on Mathesius 1926, 1943), or as a situation pronoun (Bartošová & Kučerová, 2014; Kučerová & Bartošová, 2016; Bartošová, 2017). The empirical support for this comparison comes from the observation that to is mostly restricted to inanimate antecedents. Yet, it allows animate antecedents in a limited set of environments. Moreover, to seems to combine properties of a referential pronoun and a situation-denoting pronoun. This paper argues that what distinguishes these two demonstrative types is not their internal makeup but their position in the structure. In particular, we will assume without further discussion that the agreeing type occupies an argument position, and in turn can be accounted for by, for example, Panagiotidis (2002), building on Postal (1969), and Elbourne (2008). We argue, however, that to is not an argument. Instead, to is an overt topical element merged in the MiddleField (Frey, 2000). We will use this structural configuration to explain the mixed referential behaviour attested with to. Under our account this mixed behaviour is not a property of to itself but arises from an interaction with a covert pronoun bound by to, the actual argument. The proposal explains some puzzling restrictions on the syntactic distribution and interpretation of to in quantificational environments, copular clauses, and wh-questions, and advances our understanding of topic environments and of the covert elements employed in them.

records.title: Classificatory Copular Clauses. Evidence from Czech
records.abstract: This paper discusses a novel class of NP1-NP2 copular clauses that combine properties of predicational and identificational clauses, such as This tree is a linden tree. We call such clauses classificatory copular clauses, since their NP 2 classifies the referent of NP 1 . In Czech, these clauses display a surprising syntactic behavior: even though NP 2 is not the subject and is not obviously referential, these clauses systematically display NP2 ϕ-feature agreement – both copular and inter-sentential anaphoric agreement. Building on the classificatory meaning of these clauses and their restrictive syntactic profile, we argue that the agreement is mediated by a complex covert pronoun in the Middlefield topic position. Not only does the pronoun become the vehicle of agreement, but its primary function is to enable NP2 to classify an already classified referent. We further argue that whether classificatory clauses display distinct morphosyntactic behavior in a language depends on whether that language utilizes v as the primary ϕ

records.title: 一种跨学科方法于汉藏语系研究的运用
records.abstract: Research on the Sino-Tibetan language family has spanned over a century . However, existing studies have largely remained within the linguistic domain, paying insufficient attention to the ecological transformations accompanying the diversification of Proto-Sino-Tibetan. This paper proposes an interdisciplinary methodology integrating archaeology, paleoclimatology, and natural history, organized around problem-driven inquiry rather than a single disciplinary paradigm,illustrated through specific lexical case studies. The Proto-Sino-Tibetan population can be broadly associated with the Peiligang-Yangshao cultural sequence, flourishing during the Holocene Climatic Optimum when Central China was approximately 2–3°C warmer than today, with tropical fauna such as Asian elephants, rhinoceroses, and Chinese alligators widely distributed. As Tibeto-Burman groups migrated onto the Tibetan Plateau, dramatic ecological shifts led to the loss of certain proto-roots, semantic drift, or substrate residue. Through case studies of elephant, rhinoceros, snake, crocodilian, millet, and agricultural tool terms, this paper demonstrates how ecological, climatic, and subsistence changes shaped Sino-Tibetan lexical evolution. Integrating molecular anthropological evidence, it further proposes that certain Tibetan terms for endemic species (e.g., yak g.yag, snow leopard gsa') may constitute substrate residue from D-lineage hunter-gatherer populations. This methodology, rooted in the natural history tradition while embracing modern scientific results, offers a new interdisciplinary perspective for Sino-Tibetan studies.Comments are welcome. 汉藏语系的相关研究，距今已经跨越百年。然而既有研究多囿于语言学范畴，对原始汉藏语分化过程中伴随的生态剧变关注不足。本文提出一种结合考古学、古气候学与博物学的跨学科研究方法，以“问题为中心”而非以单一学科范式为中心，并结合具体词例加以说明。 原始汉藏语人群大致归属裴李岗—仰韶文化序列，其生存时期正值全新世大暖期，中原地区 年均温较今高约 2—3℃，亚洲象、犀牛、扬子鳄等热带动物广泛分布。随着藏缅语人群迁 入青藏高原，生存生态发生显著变迁，导致部分祖语词根丢失、语义漂移或发生底层残留。 本文通过“大象”“犀牛”“蛇”“鳄”“粟黍”及农具类词例，论证生态—气候—生计方 式变迁对汉藏语词汇演变的影响；并结合分子人类学证据，提出藏语中部分本土物种词汇（如牦牛 g.yag、雪豹 gsa'）可能为 D 系狩猎采集人群的底层残留。该方法论根植于博物学传统，兼容现代技术成果，旨在为汉藏语系研究提供新的跨学科视角。欢迎批评指正。

records.title: On Differential Object Marking in Levantine Arabic: Grammatical marking in service of discourse management
records.abstract: This paper contributes to the debate on how grammatical marking shapes discourse management. Focusing on Differential Object Marking (DOM) in Levantine Arabic, we argue that DOM in this language signals the asserted proposition as a non-default Discourse Commitment (Gunlogson, 2001; Farkas and Bruce, 2010). We show that DOM triggers a range of interpretive outcomes–including emotive content, corrections, accommodations, and activating parallel Questions Under Discussion–and that the concept of a non-default Discourse Commitment accurately captures this diversity. Building on Zarka (2024), who proposes that the syntactic structure of DOM supports an aboutness topicality interpretation and provides an anaphoric anchor for adding the proposition to the Table (a discourse-tracking device), we explain why not all aboutness topics in the language yield these effects. We contend that the additional illocutionary force arises from economy considerations (Sichel and Wiltschko, 2021), because a simpler structure could otherwise express the same denotation. Our proposal reﬁnes our understanding of the structural underpinnings of non-default Discourse Commitments and underscores the role of anaphoricity in this process.

records.title: You're the only one who unifies
records.abstract: This squib concerns fake indexicals, i.e., 1st and 2nd person pronouns interpreted as bound variables. Speciﬁcally, it examines two well-known contrasts between fake indexicals associated with focus in matrix clauses and in so-called Partee sentences— relative clauses introduced by who. I argue that the locus of the cross-linguistic variation lies in which phase head has the capacity to transmit features (building on insights from Kratzer 2009, Wurmbrand 2017b, among others). The distribution is further mediated by features of the relative pronoun in the language. Englishinternal variation is a function of derivational timing, with the contribution of focus (modeled via the Exh operator of Fox 2007) playing a critical role. I suggest that, despite the differences, the Exh mechanism and the feature-transmission mechanism may be formally related: merging the Exh operator at the phase edge yields a syntactic representation that is a special case of a more general feature-uniﬁcation procedure induced on the feature structure of a phase head.

records.title: Classificatory Copular Clauses. Evidence from Czech
keywords: copular clauses; np2 agreement; classificatory clauses
records.abstract: This paper discusses a novel class of NP1-NP2 copular clauses that combine properties of predicational and identificational clauses, such as This tree is a linden tree. We call such clauses classificatory copular clauses, since their NP2 classifies the referent of NP1. In Czech, these clauses display a surprising syntactic behavior: even though NP2 is not the subject and is not obviously referential, these clauses systematically display NP2 ϕ-feature agreement – both copular and inter-sentential anaphoric agreement. Building on the classificatory meaning of these clauses and their restrictive syntactic profile, we argue that the agreement is mediated by a complex covert pronoun in the Middlefield topic position. Not only does the pronoun become the vehicle of agreement, but its primary function is to enable NP2 to classify an already classified referent. We further argue that whether classificatory clauses display distinct morphosyntactic behavior in a language depends on whether that language utilizes v as the primary ϕ-feature probe.

records.title: On (Semantic) Pleonastic and Expletive Categories in Grammar: The Cases of Vocative Particles, Vocative Phrases, Coordination, Negation, and Clitics
records.abstract: This paper addresses the issue of (semantic) pleonastic—or expletive—categories in natural lan- guages, with a focus on Italian, a language rich in such expressions. Pleonastic categories refer to elements that do not affect the truth-value conditions associated with a sentence. Examples include vocative particles, vocative phrases, coordination, expletive negations, and ethical datives. The paper presents a syntactic analysis showing that a “pleonastic/expletive” interpretation arises from a common structural configuration: these elements are directly merged in the complementizer domain (or higher), which prevents them from participating in the compositional semantics that determines propositional meaning. Instead, they contribute only to the interpretive layer, where discourse-level meanings are established. It follows that no truly semantically empty categories exist in the linguistic system; rather, their pleonastic or expletive semantics result from their syntactic configuration—and, in fact, they always retain some aspect of their original function.

records.title: Floating Quantifiers as Determiner Heads: Movement and Stranding of Arabic kull and English all
records.abstract: This dissertation investigates the floating quantifiers phenomenon, aiming to solve cases in which a universal quantifier surfaces separated from its associate nominal while preserving a tight interpretive equivalence, focusing on Arabic kull and English all. Building on the DP-hypothesis and a layered nominal architecture, the dissertation advances the central claim that universal quantifiers are best analyzed as D-heads inside DP, rather than as VP-adjunct adverbs or as Q-heads of a QP layer. Under this view, the quantifier and its associate are not autonomous phrases, they form a unified constituent, and the surface ‘adverbial-like’ placements characteristic of floating are derived via nominal movement that strands the quantifier in an intermediate landing position. Empirically, Arabic morphosyntax is leveraged as a decisive diagnostic through its agreement morphology and pronominal clitics in floated configurations, constituency and dependency predictions are tested. Arabic provides evidence for constituency, landing positions, and a canonical post-verbal clause-final Q position, base-generating the quantifier and it associate in the verbal domain. To address cross-linguistic variation, such as the availability of clause-final floated quantifiers in Arabic but not in English, the dissertation proposes a derivational model that (i) identifies a universal canonical base-position for Q and its associate DP in the verbal spine, (ii) restricts the derivation to a constrained set of landing sites and movement paths, and (iii) captures language differences via ON/OFF switch settings that license or block specific surface realizations of Q and its DP. Finally, this dissertation moves toward a broader account of the DP Hypothesis by arguing that DP structure should be maintained even in determiner-less languages. Together with the proposed account of quantifier’s canonical base-position, movement and stranding, this DP-based view aims to contribute to a unified analysis of floating quantifiers across languages. While the dissertation does not claim to establish a universal theory of floating quantifiers, it aims toward a more general, potentially universal framework based on shared structural principles across languages.

records.title: Investigating contrastive inference generation across speech and gesture
records.abstract: This paper investigates whether the generation of contrastive inferences depends on the at-issue status of a modifier or on its semiotic status. We report a German adaptation of the picture-selection paradigm developed by Alsop et al. (2018) and extend it to include pro-speech gestures. Participants completed a picture-selection task with three experimental conditions (lexical modifiers, pro-speech gestures, and co-speech gestures). In addition, each list contained unmodified baseline items that were not part of the factorial design. The results revealed a gradient pattern: lexical modifiers elicited the highest rate of contrastive interpretations, followed by pro-speech gestures and co-speech gestures. At the same time, both gesture conditions yielded substantially more contrastive interpretations than the control condition. We argue that these findings support a gradient, context-sensitive view of at-issueness while at the same time challenging accounts that exclude depictive meaning from alternative-based reasoning.

records.title: 藏缅语族“马”词的 BMAC 中介假说——基于考古学与历史语言学的新证据
records.abstract: Abstract: This paper is an extension of the working paper “The Origin of the Old Chinese Word for‘horse’: An Indo-European Loanword Hypothesis via a Yeniseian Intermediary.” The Tibeto-Burman words for “horse” are formally divergent—Tibetan rta, rGyalrong mbrō, and Limbu ən—and are difficult to correlate with one another; they also cannot be phonologically matched with Chinese **mˤraʔ*. Combining Zhang et al.’s (2019) data on the divergence depth of Tibeto-Burman, Lyonnet’s (2021) archaeological study of the BMAC, and the material evidence for the southward migration of the Sintashta-Andronovo culture, this paper proposes that the Tibeto-Burman word for “horse” may have been transmitted through a BMAC intermediary. As the area of most intensive contact between southern Central Asia and steppe populations ca. 2200–1500 BCE, the BMAC is the most likely intermediary on chronological, geographical, and archaeological grounds. Since the linguistic affiliation of the BMAC remains uncertain, this paper does not attempt to reconstruct a proto-form; rather, it argues primarily from archaeological evidence for the plausibility of the BMAC as an intermediary. This is a working paper; comments are welcome. 摘要：本文是工作论文“上古汉语“马”的来源——一个经叶尼塞语系中介的印欧语借词假说”的延伸讨论。藏缅语族“马”词形式迥异：藏语 rta、嘉绒语 mbrō、林布语ən，彼此难以对应，亦与汉语 mˤraʔ在音系上无法匹配。本文结合张梦翰等（2019）关于藏缅语分化深度的数据、Lyonnet（2021）对 BMAC 的考古学研究，以及辛塔什塔-安德罗诺沃文化南迁的物质证据提出：藏缅语的“马”词可能经 BMAC 中介传入。BMAC 作为约公元前 2200–1500 年间中亚南部与草原人群接触最密集的区域，在时间、地理和考古证据上都是最可能的中介。由于BMAC 语言归属尚不明确，本文不试图重构原始形式，而主要从考古学角度论证 BMAC 作为中介的合理性。本文为工作论文，欢迎批评。

records.title: Learning What to Leave Unsaid: Acquisition Setting, Cross- Linguistic Influence and the Implicit Goal in L3 Narratives
records.abstract: When people learn a new language, they learn more than its grammar. They may also learn what its speakers usually leave unsaid. I tested this idea with the LnNor Corpus, in which the same Polish speakers told picture stories in Polish, in English (their second language) and in Norwegian (their third). Twenty-nine had learned English and Norwegian in the classroom; twenty-three had learned them by living in Norway. Classroom learners often stated what the characters wanted (the cat wants the fish), and did so more in English and Norwegian than in Polish. Learners who lived in Norway also stated it freely in Polish, but almost never in English or Norwegian (p < .001 and p = .002). There they described only the attempt (the cat tries to catch the fish) and left the goal to be inferred, as native speakers did. Three further tests clarify the pattern. It was not carried over from the speakers' first or second language: it followed where the languages had been learned. It was not explained by speakers treating the task as a picture description. And it went with fluency, not with signs of difficulty. Read through Relevance Theory and Learnable Theory, leaving the goal implicit is an efficient choice, learned from the community that speaks the language. The results are exploratory, and I propose a replication and physiological tests of whether listeners reconstruct the unstated goal.

records.title: When I am you: Deriving honorifics through weak indices
records.abstract: Honorifics across languages tend to recruit specific phi-features (e.g. plural and 3rd person) for polite reference to the addressee. Wang (2023) derives this regularity pragmatically from the interaction between Maximize Presupposition! and a Taboo of Directness over the presuppositionally weak features "plural" and "3rd person". We argue that this account both undergenerates and overgenerates. It cannot accommodate the typological asymmetries between 1st and 2nd person (e.g. the absence of speaker-inclusive 2PL), the role-specific use-conditions attached to forms like English Nurse We, the disappearance of honorific content under ellipsis, or the lexeme-specific contrasts seen, e.g., in Spanish nosotros vs. null pro. We propose a hybrid pragmatic-conventional alternative. Person and number are treated not as presuppositional heads but as components of complex anaphoric indices, with their semantic import encoded as constraints on admissible assignment functions. Assuming this system, we derive a markedness hierarchy 2 < 1 < 3 over indices defined by referential explicitness. A valence-neutral Taboo of Distance favors weak indices for the expression of social or psychological distance, while language-specific use-conditional constraints license particular weak indices in particular utterance contexts. Crucially, a conjunctive definition of semantic information over both truth-conditional and use-conditional dimensions allows weak indices enriched by conventional use-conditions to survive Quantity-based competition with their more explicit alternatives, dissolving the apparent conflict between informativity and indirectness. The result accommodates 1st person addresse honorifics, anti-honorific uses of the same features, and the existence of lexical idiosyncrasies in honorific inventories.

records.title: Translation Literacy in Asylum Interpreting: A Pilot Study of TRACE and Structured Reflection
records.abstract: Interpreting quality can shape how an asylum applicant's account is understood, while UK inspection and guidance documents continue to identify challenges involving language matching, interpreter preparation and quality assurance. This pilot study operationalises translation literacy as explicit reflection on translation choices, semantic range, alternatives, evidence, consequences and evaluation. Twenty-one Arabic-English bilingual adults completed unguided pre- and post-framework translation-evaluation tasks after guided exposure either to TRACE, a five-step mnemonic reflection scaffold, or to an active structured control checklist. Eighty-four responses were scored on a six-dimension rubric by the original marker and three independent blinded raters; analyses used the mean of the four ratings. TRACE did not produce a statistically significant advantage over control on combined change scores (TRACE +1.48/24; control +2.33/24; U=47.0, p=.597). Alternatives showed the clearest TRACE-aligned descriptive pattern, but the between-group change difference was non-significant. The findings therefore do not establish TRACE superiority or a general causal effect of structured reflection. They instead identify a feasible measurement approach and hypotheses for larger, better-balanced studies using professional interpreters, delayed retention testing and spoken high-stakes tasks.

records.title: Two types of Modification in Mandarin Chinese NPs
records.abstract: In Mandarin Chinese, adjectives can modify nouns in two ways: (i) an adjective combines directly with a noun (A-N structure), or (ii) an adjective combines with the marker DE, and the resulting constituent modifies the nominal spine (A-DE-N structure). These two constructions exhibit a distributional asymmetry regarding simple and complex adjectives: while simple adjectives can appear in both structures, complex adjectives require the marker DE to modify a noun. This paper pursues two main goals. First, we investigate the morphosyntactic status of the two structures on the basis of their syntactic and semantic properties. We argue that A-DE-N structures are phrasal, whereas A-N structures result from morphological concatenation. Second, we develop an analysis that accounts for the attested distributional patterns and formalises the interpretational differences between A-N and A-DE-N structures. Our analysis further addresses the behaviour of reduplicated adjectives in Mandarin Chinese.

records.title: Comment on Gibson(2026a) and Some Other Reflections
records.abstract: I examined some of Gibson(2026a)'s claims and relevant claims cited there, together with some Hinton's claims concerning generative linguistics. [Disclaimer: this is a work in progress, feedback is welcome]

records.title: Hypothesis : Traces of an original language in THe Altaic Languages
records.abstract: This paper presents an independent working hypothesis proposing that the structural similarities observed across the Altaic language family—including Turkic, Mongolic, Tungusinic, Koreanic, Japonic, and Ainu languages—serve as structural traces of an original ancestral language. By examining the inherent stability of language structures over borrowed vocabulary, this paper argues that uninterrupted geographical transmission chains (such as those across the Eurasian steppe) favor the preservation of deep structural features. Consequently, despite external lexical shifts, core grammatical architectures remain remarkably resilient, offering a new perspective on macro-family relationships and linguistic evolution.

records.title: A Contrastive Analysis of the Phonological Systems of Bambara and English: Implications for Language Teaching.
records.abstract: This paper examines the phonological systems of Bambara and English from a contrastive linguistic perspective, with particular attention to their implications for language teaching and learning.
