records.title: Linguistic meaning needs stable concepts
records.abstract: Nicholas Shea’s *Concepts at the Interface* (2024) identifies concepts with temporary working memory (WM) labels: ‘two-ended’ devices connected to stored information at one end and composing with other labels at the other. I argue that this framework cannot yet account for linguistic understanding. First, Shea’s theory requires stable categorical mechanisms to track category identity over time, although he is officially neutral as to their nature. Second, even granting such mechanisms, neither they nor his temporary WM labels can provide the needed compositional vehicles. The empirical evidence I review converges on the need for stable, freely compositional vehicles that I call ‘G-concepts’. On the view developed here, G-concepts—stable symbols individuated by their compositional role—compose into thoughts and bear word meaning, while ‘S-concepts’—stable representations that underwrite categorization—orient the mind toward the world. The Hybrid view preserves Shea’s interface insight while providing the compositional resources needed for linguistic cognition.

records.title: Donkeys, bishops, and the distinction between weak and strong definites
records.abstract: **Joint work with Franco Liu** Much recent work on definiteness has assumed that definite descriptions come in two types, weak and strong. Weak definites make use of a simple situation-relative uniqueness operator; strong definites add to this a variable available to dynamic binding. Drawing on evidence from Mandarin, Jenks (2018) influentially proposed that strong definites but not weak definites can serve as donkey anaphors. We show that this claim is incorrect for Mandarin as well as for German and English. Certain special cases of donkey anaphora nevertheless have diagnostic value for the distinction between weak and strong definites. We discuss two. First, in structures where there is no dynamic quantifier available to serve as an antecedent, strong definite descriptions cannot serve as donkey anaphors. Second, in so-called bishop sentences, the uniqueness requirement of the weak definite is not met; in these cases weak definite descriptions cannot serve as donkey anaphors. We apply these tests to definites in German, English, and Mandarin. Our results indicate that English the and Mandarin bare nouns are always weak definites, but also that important aspects of crosslinguistic variation with respect to weak definites remain to be explained.

records.title: Lexical causatives and their mood choice: The curious case of recordar
records.abstract: This squib revisits the claim that causative predicates uniformly trigger subjunctive complements in Catalan (Rigau, 1981; Quer, 1998). While canonical causatives such as fer ‘make’ require subjunctive clauses, causative recordar ‘remind’ permits the indicative. We argue that mood selection is sensitive not simply to the causative semantics, but to the structural relation between the causative predicate and the embedded proposition. Whereas fer directly embeds the propositional content, recordar introduces it indirectly through a further embedded predicate that is a part of a periphrastic structure. We suggest that this layered structure fits well into the locality effects of subjunctive selection (Quer, 1998) which, in turn, predict the possibility of indicative in clausal complements of recordar.

records.title: Temperature in symbolic understanding
records.abstract: The same copular syntax that yields the tradition's favorite truth condition, \textit{snow is white}, yields the animal rights movement's favorite slogan, \textit{meat is murder}. We argue that the difference between the two lives in a single parameter of the \textit{evaluation}, temperature, and that the term is not a metaphor: the parameter so named is literally the one that Harmonic Grammar and maximum entropy phonotactics fit to gradient acceptability data. The attention mechanism of transformers runs at the fixed temperature $1/\sqrt{d}$, and deployed language models expose a second instance of the same parameter to their users as the sampling knob. Grammaticality stars, analytic truths, thematic role assignment, anaphora resolution, and rhetorical force are readouts of one Gibbs competition at different operating points. We work through the mechanism on \textit{meat is murder} and its political cousins \textit{property is theft} and \textit{taxation is theft}, and on anaphora resolution in \textit{he beat him} discourses and Winograd schemas. A small experiment on a deployed model tells the two sites of the parameter apart: the sampling knob leaves the reading of \textit{meat is murder} untouched at every setting, the evaluation instruction flips it, and the model's refusal, when it refuses, localizes at the one taught boundary the analysis predicts. A self-contained appendix develops the machinery -- Gibbs distributions, annealing, energy landscapes, softmax, regularization -- assuming nothing beyond linear algebra and one-variable calculus.

records.title: Puzzles in pronominal structure from Nord-Jæren
records.abstract: This paper focuses on pronouns in the Norwegian dialects spoken in the Nord-Jæren region, a geographic area in Rogaland county on the Norwegian West Coast. We present a data set focusing on three variants of the 3rd person feminine singular object pronoun ("her"): hu, 'na and henna. We raise the question how these three variants fit into pronominal typologies such as Cardinaletti & Starke's (1996, 1999) classification of pronouns as clitic, weak and strong. We present a survey where participants (n=822) were asked to choose which of the three pronouns fits best in a given sentence. The survey results indicate that 'na is the unmarked form, whereas hu and henna are preferred in a subset of contexts, such as the topic position and the complement position of a copula verb. The overall data are indicative of a markedness hierarchy (from least marked to most marked): 'na < hu < henna. Within this markedness hierarchy, both hu and henna pattern as strong pronouns in the sense of Cardinaletti & Starke (1996, 1999), whereas 'na qualifies as a weak pronoun. These generalizations lay the groundwork for further exploration into the morphosyntactic properties of the Nord-Jæren dialects, which bears on the question of how pronominal systems are organized cross-linguistically, particularly whether languages can have more than one pronominal paradigm that classifies as strong.

records.title: A note on Nacireman suprasegmental phonology
records.abstract: This note discusses some recent findings in Nacireman phonology. This language makes suprasegmental use of overtones on each syllable to encode lexical meaning. This typologically unusual feature is integrated into several morphological alternations in the language.

records.title: Clausal nominalization in Ka(g)wahíva
records.abstract: Clausal nominalizations, which combine nominal properties externally with verbal properties internally, have often been understood as involving a nominal layer above the clausal content (Borsley & Kornfilt 2000; Kornfilt & Whitman 2011). Research based on this assumption proposes that the nominal layer consists of a determiner element D that nominalizes the clause structure rather than an n (or N). In this paper, I argue that clausal nominalizations do not always require a DP layer. Furthermore, I demonstrate that TP-nominalizations by nP do exist. I support both claims by examining nominalized complement clauses in the Tupí-Guaraní language Ka(g)wahíva. I show that complement clauses in this language are nominalized through nP, and do not have any additional nominal projections. Moreover, the clausal content consists solely of a TP. The first finding parallels clausal nominalization in Japanese and the Mongolic language Khalkha (Nasu et al. 2024; Lim 2025), while the second finding has only been argued for the Bantu language Oshiwambo (Lee & Ndapo 2025).

records.title: The Password
records.abstract: A reader who encounters the companion papers without this piece will find rigorous argument: convergence across Halliday's linguistics, gerontolinguistic evidence, phenomenological philosophy, developmental psychology. The argument stands on its own. But what precedes it is the encounter that made the argument findable at all — a man in an apartment, three years into living inside cultural difference, reading a novel about the first men who held hafts, and feeling something arrive that the categories he had spent his career building could not hold. The haft was always resting in a hand. The password was always waiting in the ivory. What the years built was the capacity to feel it when it arrived.

records.title: Undiscoverable meanings: Presupposition and the limits of word learning
records.abstract: Children are remarkable word learners, who exploit a variety of information sources — syntax, others’ attention and intention, general expectations about communication — to learn otherwise hidden meanings. Here we explore the learning of presupposition triggers, a ubiquitous but special class of words whose meanings cannot be learned from the usual information sources. In their syntactic distribution, they overlap with presupposition-free counterparts, and their meaning includes information that everyone in the conversation takes for granted, making it unattended and uninformative by definition. How, then, do children figure out that this information is part of a word’s meaning, let alone that it is presupposed? We decompose the problem of presupposition learning into two components: discovery (registering that the presupposed content is part of the word’s meaning) and packaging (determining that it is presupposed rather than asserted). If all the child ever encountered were typical uses of triggers, the problem of discovery might indeed be unsolvable. We propose that presuppositions are instead discovered from atypical, informative uses. The packaging problem, in contrast, is solved using typical uses, with various sources of evidence bearing on it. Separating discovery from packaging makes the problem tractable and yields predictions about the course of learning, the evidence that drives it, and the intermediate meanings learners may entertain. Beyond development, the decomposition relocates the hard question, from how meanings get assigned their dimension to how presupposed content becomes representable at all. It offers an instructive test case for psychological accounts that tie word learning to communicative usefulness.

records.title: Typicality in referent choice: what the description leaves open
records.abstract: A description built on a superordinate category term (an animal perched on a branch) does not pick out its members evenly: some come to mind more readily than others. This paper separates three conditions under which such a description meets two candidate referents differing in typicality, according to whether the full description is satisfied by both, by the atypical candidate only, or by the typical candidate only. These conditions support different interpretations of the same choice response and therefore require separate analysis. Forced-choice referent selection is the appropriate primary instrument for comparing them, but choice alone cannot separate a candidate rejected as false from one rejected as a worse fit, so judgment data remain necessary. Picture-based versions add a further confound: the restricting detail must be visually recoverable before it can override anything. An existing image-based study is described as a worked instance. No new results are reported.

records.title: Grice at the Border
records.abstract: An asylum answer may be judged evasive before anyone establishes whether the applicant understood the question. This article uses Grice's Cooperative Principle to examine how a judgement about an answer's relevance, detail or expression becomes a judgement about the speaker's truthfulness. I call this movement pragmatic credibility migration. Drawing on research into asylum communication and four published UK decisions, I distinguish misunderstanding, limited knowledge, interpreting error and the later misreading of a record. I argue that assessors should identify the proposition attributed to an applicant, show how the record supports it and address any explanation for the apparent difficulty. Communicative safety names the conditions in which uncertainty and correction can be examined as evidence without deciding credibility in advance.

records.title: On semantic plurality within the Spanish DP and ad sensum agreement:  A Count-based mechanism for combinatorial variability
records.abstract: In Spanish ad sensum agreement, semantically-plural, but grammatically-singular subjects, of the form [DP1 [de NP2/DP2]] 'DP1 of NP2/DP2' (e.g. la mayoría de los triunfadores ‘the majority of the winners’), agree with a singular or plural verb. Previous accounts identify a ‘head N’ responsible for agreement, but cannot explain variable agreement. We couch our proposal within Distributed Morphology (DM), with number encoded and valued semantically and morphologically, following research on DP-internal gender (e.g. Kramer 2016, Puškar 2018). We propose that conflicting semantic and morphological number within the DP triggers Count, an alternative agreement mechanism that calculates a plural ratio diacritic for variable production based on feature values. We test our hypothesis comparing predicted rates of singular and plural verb agreement generated by Count with attested data in the Corpus del Español (CdE). Statistical analysis reveals that the variables in our proposal are significant predictors of variable agreement observed in the data.

records.title: Patterns in Chaos: Composite A'/A Probes
records.abstract: This thesis presents a comparative study of composite A'/A constructions and develops a syntactic analysis for investigating such constructions cross-linguistically. In many languages, phrasal movement falls into two types with mutually exclusive properties: A-movement (e.g. passivization) and A'-movement (e.g. wh-movement, topicalization). Some languages, however, exhibit movement that combines properties associated with both types. In recent featural approaches, such derivations have commonly been analyzed as involving a composite [A'/A] probe, suggesting that phrasal movement can be triggered by a fused [A'/A] probe and thereby form an A'/A chain. The thesis systematically compares composite constructions in fifteen languages from nine language families, including Dinka Bor extraction, Mandarin Chinese BEI passives and TP-internal topics/foci, Khanty passives, promotion to pivot in Balinese and Malagasy, as well Hyperraising, and long-distance agreement in various languages. I ask whether A'/A constructions exhibit arbitrary combinations of A'- and A-properties or whether these properties follow predictable distributions. I show that only a small number of A'/A mixtures is attested cross-linguistically and that these follow a highly systematic pattern: some A'- and A-properties consistently cluster together, while others allow more variation. Based on these findings, I develop a unified syntax of composite [A'/A] probes that differs from existing accounts in proposing that there is no such thing as "composite A'/A movement". Although [A] and [A'] features may combine on a single probe and jointly search for a goal, the resulting movement chain is either an A-chain or an A'-chain, never a mixed chain. I therefore reconceptualize the traditional binary A'/A distinction as a finer-grained, tripartite system involving three interacting factors: i) the probing head ([A'], [A], or [A'/A]), ii) the movement chain (A or A'), and iii) the location of the probing head in the syntactic spine (on C or below). Each factor determines a distinct subset of A'- and A-properties. Their different combinations give rise to what I term a construction-specific A'/A signature, which predicts the particular combination of properties associated with a given construction. While natural language permits only a limited number of such signatures, this set is larger than the traditional binary A'/A distinction. I apply the A'/A signature analysis to established [A'/A] probe accounts in Dinka Bor, Mandarin Chinese, and Khanty, and extend it to Hyperraising, long-distance agreement, and promotion to pivot in Balinese and Malagasy. The analysis captures the composite nature of these constructions while maintaining a unified account of their properties. Beyond the analysis of A'/A signatures, the thesis addresses broader questions concerning the emergence of composite [A'/A] probes, the implications of a featural approach to phrasal movement, the nature of A'- and A-movement, and the role of comparative syntax.

records.title: Referential readings of reflexives
records.abstract: I show that reflexives in DP-sized Right Node Raising pivots can have strict readings, just like pronouns in the same environment. Certain properties of these examples preclude an elliptical analysis of Right Node Raising. A multidominant analysis of these examples follows if we assume strict readings come from a referential reading of these reflexives and pronouns. This paper thus supports a treatment of reflexives that distinguish referential from bound readings. Reflexives are like pronouns, except they have to satisfy Condition A. (This paper is titled "Rediscovering referential reflexives with Right Node Raising" in its later iterations.)

records.title: Embedded Reciprocal Equatives in Mandarin and Semantic Weakening
records.abstract: In this paper I present a novel observation on reciprocal equatives (henceforth, RE) in Mandarin: a reciprocal equative, when embedded under a necessity modal or a predicate of desire, gives rise to an unexpected, at-least-equal-to interpretation (henceforth, ≥-interpretation). I show that the meaning of a modal sentence or a desire report of this kind may be derived through the postulation of two covert operators: one is akin to at least and serves to weaken the meaning of the embedded RE; the other is an exhaustification operator, which gives rise to the inference of sufficiency. Along with Alonso-Ovalle and Hirsch’s (2022) analysis, the proposal draws a connection between the sufficiency modal construction (e.g., To get good cheese, you only have to go to the North Ends) and examples of embedded reciprocal equatives investigated in this paper. To the extent that the proposal is on the right track, it provides further support for the postulation of a semantic weakening operator in natural language meaning composition and sheds light on the issue how this weakening operation may be constrained (e.g., Alonso-Ovalle and Hirsch, 2022; Crniˇc, 2011; Schwarz, 2005).

records.title: What Frequency Matching Might (not) Be
records.abstract: Frequency matching has been proposed as a central principle underlying phonological knowledge and learning. A central example comes from Hungarian vowel harmony, where stems with back vowels followed by neutral vowel(s) show structurally-conditioned lexical variation in whether they take back or front suffixes. In wug tests, Hungarian speakers show evidence of internalizing this structural conditioning, often taken as evidence of speakers internalizing a probabilistic grammar. This article critically analyzes the Frequency Matching Hypothesis and argues that the appearance of frequency matching emerges from variation across speaker vocabularies and from averaging over categories that may not reflect those internalized by speakers. I suggest that the central question of lexical variation is how learners discover its structural conditioning and propose a learning theory, in the form of an independently-motivated learning model, for that question. Assuming just variation across speaker vocabularies, the model exhibits the appearance of frequency matching. The model matches wug test results as well as previously proposed probabilistic grammars, predicts a diachronic shift in Hungarian vowel transparency, and explains a surprising lack of token-level variation in Hungarian vowel harmony.

records.title: On declarative and polar complements in Persian
records.abstract: In Persian, anti-rogative predicates can select for an embedded clause with the polarity particle aya in certain contexts. We characterize these contexts as non-veridical, and we propose that the particle does not introduce a polar question: the ke aya-complement denotes a unique proposition and conveys that the latter is positively or negatively decided in the attitude state of the selecting anti-rogative predicate. In veridical contexts, the ke aya-complement is ruled out by the competition of the corresponding declarative complement, which conveys positive decidedness and thus determines strictly more informative truth conditions. In non-veridical contexts, however, the informativeness competition is suspended and ke aya-complements are allowed. We argue that the polar complement interpretation constitutes a weakening of the interpretation of aya as the polar question operator.

records.title: Deconstructing glottalization, ejectivity, and breathy voice in Armenian dialects
records.abstract: Previous work has reported that several Armenian varieties show ejective or glottalized stops, a claim with significant implications for the reconstruction of the Proto-Indo-European stop system. This paper reviews the historical, dialectological, and phonetic evidence for ejective, glottalized, and breathy-voiced stops in Armenian, finding that these claims largely rest on unreliable impressionistic reports. To provide an empirical assessment, we present preliminary acoustic data from field recordings of three native speakers of the Janik subdialect of Hamshen Armenian. This variety has previously been reported to possess glottalized / ejective stops, and we additionally test whether its historical voiced series is realized with breathy phonation. We conducted an exploratory acoustic analysis by extracting fundamental frequency (F0) trajectories and Cepstral Peak Prominence (CPP) values at the vowel onset following target plosives. Our initial findings yield no clear evidence of full glottal closure or severe aperiodicity associated with glottalization or ejectivity, nor of the laryngeal slackness associated with breathy voice. Instead, the target tokens predominantly exhibit high-falling F0 trajectories and CPP values characteristic of modal voice. While further large-scale articulatory and statistical work is needed, these preliminary results suggest that where non-modal phonation or ejectivity does occur in Armenian, it is likely sporadic or paralinguistic, offering little support for the existence of a stable ejective, glottalized, or breathy-voiced series.

records.title: External arguments in the short passive? The view from Spanish
records.abstract: In this paper, we examine the status of the syntactic projection of the implicit external argument in short periphrastic passive derivations in Spanish. To do this, we apply tests mainly from Collins (2005, 2024) concerning the licensing of agent-oriented secondary depictive predicates, the argument control of big PRO subjects of embedded clauses, the binding of reflexive pronominals, and the non-anaphoric status of non-reflexive pronominals. The results of these tests, placed in a theoretical context of a Minimalist framework (e.g., Chomsky 2021; Chomsky et al. 2023), strongly endorse a view in which the external argument is syntactically-projected in the Spanish short passive. We additionally present novel evidence from Spanish that the reflexive pronominal elements licensed in Spanish short passives cannot plausibly be exempt logophors. In accordance with these theoretical and empirical considerations, we straightforwardly adopt Collins’ (2005, 2024) smuggling approach to the Spanish passive. We further show that several notable properties of the Spanish passive are naturally explained under this smuggling analysis, such as the preverbal, nominative status of the structural subject, the obligatory agreement in phi-features between the participial verb and the subject, and the impossibility of inalienable-possession readings of the short passive, as noted by MacDonald (2017).

records.title: Hey, wait a minute! If scalar implicatures are presupposed, why do they fail the “Hey, wait a minute!” test?
records.abstract: It has recently been argued that scalar implicatures are presuppositional; e.g. that the inference of the sentence "some students passed the test" that not all students passed the test is a presupposition of the sentence (Bassi et al., 2021). A known challenge to this approach is that scalar implicatures do not intuitively feel like presuppositions, and, more concretely, do not pass a well known test that diagnoses presuppositional content; the "Hey, wait a minute! I didn't know that..." test (Shanon 1976, von Fintel 2004). We offer a new way of thinking about this diagnostic that renders the fact that it does not seem to target implicatures unproblematic for their presuppositional analysis.

records.title: The Pure Truth About Latin S Impurum: Exposing the Fiction of Extrasyllabicity
records.abstract: In Latin phonology and poetry, so-called s impurum refers chiefly to word-initial s + stop clusters, e.g. in stā.re ‘to stand’. When preceded by a vowel, the cluster is heterosyllabic, e.g. /re + stāre/ res.tā.re ‘to remain’. To make sense of this apparent inconsistency, Cser (2012) posits that this medial s is “extrasyllabic” but that a stipulation prohibiting extrasyllabic segments from neighboring a nucleus obliges it to become a coda via “leftward resyllabification.” Parker (2002:9) considers this contrivance “painful.” Rejecting the inherently exceptional “extrasyllabic” analysis of s impurum, this paper proposes an exception-free Optimality Theoretic (OT) account relying solely on necessary, cross-linguistic generalizations. Hierarchically arranged, these constraints collaboratively drive the syllabification of every s, each syllabification being the best fit for its respective environment. Notably, the constraint hierarchy never references the segment [s]. A testament to the robust coherence and parsimony of this analysis, the same constraint hierarchy—without modifications or stipulations—(1) accounts for the exceptional behavior of other clusters (ps, mn); (2) elucidates the seemingly exceptional effect of x on meter; and (3) refutes the supposed “unknowability” of whether the purportedly extrasyllabic, “trapped” [s] in e.g. dexter [dekster] ‘right’ is an onset or coda (Cser 2016). Additionally, the paper critiques the argumentation underpinning the extrasyllabicity account by identifying several overlapping fallacies that undermine the hypothesis. The study also examines why Latin poets avoided s impurum in “non-neutral” positions, e.g. un.de.#ski.at (in Lucretius) vs. nul.la#s.pēs (Catullus), speculating on the cognitive and sociolinguistic benefits afforded by the avoidance of this superficially ambiguous structure. Though poets avoided non-neutral s impurum, their distinct preferences for syllabifying it as an onset vs. coda are depicted here in terms of the optimal output of – very simply – two ways to rank the same constraint set. The analysis underscores the importance of prioritizing necessary generalizations over ad hoc stipulations in phonological analysis and offers insights into a dilemma faced by the poets. Demonstrating economy, elegance, and intuitive appeal, the proposed OT approach dispels the pejorative taint traditionally associated with s "impurum" and illustrates that its syllabification ceases to be a curiosity when examined through the lens of OT tableaux.

records.title: Experimental evidence for partial conjunct agreement in Turkish
records.abstract: In several languages, when a head agrees with a conjoined phrase, it may express either the sum of the features of all conjuncts (i.e., full agreement) or the features of only a subset of conjuncts (i.e., partial agreement). Investigations into (partial) agreement with conjunction have played a crucial role in linguistic theorizing of agreement. Here we aim to contribute to this literature by experimentally investigating verbal agreement strategies with coordinate and disjunctive subjects in Turkish. Using three acceptability judgment tasks, we test the availability of partial verbal agreement with preverbal and postverbal coordinate subjects and preverbal disjunctive subjects. For coordinate subjects, we find that full agreement is the most acceptable strategy, while partial agreement with the last (or second) conjunct ‘I’ is somewhat available in both word orders. For disjunctive subjects, acceptability is overall degraded, suggesting a grammatical gap in assigning number with disjunction. Nevertheless, similar to coordination, full agreement remains the most acceptable option, followed by partial agreement with the last conjunct.

records.title: Messapic and Albanian: Linguistic Affiliation and the Age of Albanian
records.abstract: Messapic is an Indo-European language attested in inscriptions from pre-Roman Apulia. Its possible relationship with the prehistoric ancestor of Albanian remains disputed. Messapic bilia and Albanian bijë, both meaning “daughter”, offer a noteworthy comparison, but the limited corpus does not yet support a secure classification based on regular sound correspondences and shared morphological innovations. This review considers three claims often presented together: that Messapic and Albanian are related, that Messapic was Albanian’s closest ancient relative, and that Messapic can establish the age of Albanian. The first is uncontroversial at the broad Indo-European level; a particularly close relationship is plausible but not established; the third claim does not follow. The earliest surviving Albanian texts are late medieval, whereas the spoken language has a much older prehistory.

records.title: Refining the internal structure of expressive binominal structures: a view from Italian
records.abstract: Several languages display Qualitative Binominal Noun Phrases (QBNPs), i.e. binominal structures where the first noun phrase encodes an evaluation by the speaker of the referent denoted by the second noun phrase, and at the same time conveys the emotional state of the speaker. An example of such a structure is given in (1), which conveys the fact that the speaker is annoyed by a professor, for whatever reason. (1) That idiot of a professor has disappeared again! We argue that Italian provides evidence for the existence of (at least) three different classes of Expressive Nouns (EN), which differ from each other in terms of (i) semantic and pragmatic contribution to the proposition, (ii) syntactic distribution, and (iii) concord patterns. The QBNPs we discuss feature ENs such as cazzo ‘dick’, merda ‘shit’, and stronzo ‘turd’ (2). We propose that the different ENs we identify occupy different syntactic positions, i.e. they can occur in the specifier of a functional projection hosting evaluative adjectives or in the Deg-head hosted in the extended projection of such functional projection. We also propose that the expressive component of these ENs is determined by both their syntactic position and the degree to which they are grammaticalised. More specifically, we argue that their different behaviour with respect to concord derives from their morpho-syntactic structure, namely from the hypothesis that ENs can be semi-lexical to different degrees, and from the EN having or not having interpretable ϕ-features that can be either valued or unvalued. As for the prepositional element occurring between ENs and RNs, we propose that it is a context-dependent realisation of a morphosyntactic structure that is formally and functionally similar to adjectival concord markers.

records.title: Restricting resolutions: effect-driven semantics of numerical approximation
records.abstract: Approximators such as approximately or exactly have been analyzed either as operators that manipulate a numeral's denotation, or as devices that select a granularity level at which the numeral is interpreted. A single numeral, however, can host several approximating devices at once. In Ukrainian, an overt adverb, a preposition, an indefinite, and approximative inversion may co-occur with one numeral, yet the result conveys the same interval as any one alone, differing only in an intensified hedging effect. Pragmatic halo theories correctly predict that imprecision in such cases does not compound, but fail to rule out mixed-precision stacks like approximately exactly; granularity-based accounts predict that stacking is infelicitous altogether. I propose an approach where a single mechanism derives the idempotence of same-precision stacking alongside the phenomena prior views miss. I argue that a bare numeral introduces a family of resolution descriptions—the precision levels at which it may be read—and approximators function like indefinites and definites over this family: approximately restricts it to its non-exact members without choosing among them, and exactly retrieves the unique exact member. Stacking is then intersection of conditions, idempotent for same-precision devices and contradictory for mixed-precision ones. I implement the account in effect-driven semantics and lift it to probabilistic dynamic semantics. Treating the choice of resolution as uncertain yields an interpretation peaked at the numeral; roundness and magnitude phenomena then reduce to how the prior over resolutions varies with it. The mixed-precision clash is rescued in discourse as an instance of ordinary anaphora.

records.title: Why sound change begins: pressure, resistance and actuation
records.abstract: This work proposes a mechanistic model of sound change based on pressure-resistance dynamics and tipping-point behaviour. It explains how small phonetic biases can accumulate, stall, or suddenly accelerate, producing the historical patterns seen in vowel shifts, rhoticity loss, and regional diffusion, etc. The mechanism links sociophonetic evolution and offers a unified framework for understanding when and why sound change progresses. https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22712648 The full licence information is available on the Zenodo DOI page linked above

records.title: The Licensing of Nominal and Verbal Ellipsis in Romanian
records.abstract: The goal of this work is to provide a description and an in-depth analysis of the main configurations in which nominal ellipsis and verbal ellipsis are licensed in Romanian. Chapter I provides a motivation for the choice of nominal and verbal Following previous bibliography, I focus on a particular family of elliptical types, namely elliptical structures which (i) are derived by PF-deletion and (ii) are tied to a particular licensing element; this class includes elliptical phenomena like sluicing, VP-ellipsis and nominal ellipsis. Chapter II discusses at length the differences between these phenomena and other types of surface anaphora (such as gapping and stripping). Chapters III and IV are devoted to the in-depth study of verbal and nominal ellipsis, and chapter V summarizes the results and puts them into a larger perspective. [This book is a revised version of my 2013 PhD dissertation (Types of Ellipsis in Romanian. The Interpretation of Structures containing Ellipsis Sites and the Syntactic Licensing of Ellipsis), jointly supervised by professors Gabriela Pană Dindelegan (University of Bucharest) and Ian Roberts (University of Cambridge). I defended this dissertation in November 2013 at the University of Bucharest, and published the monograph in 2019 with Bucharest University Press.]

records.title: Reanalyzing perfects: The definite article and the rise of Romance HAVE-auxiliaries
records.abstract: We propose a formal syntactic analysis of the Latin construction at the origin of Romance perfect tenses with a have-auxiliary, arguing that the Latin construction ‘habere + NP.acc + PaPa.acc’ is a grammatically passive structure in which habere ‘have’ is the main verb, selecting a small clause with the accusative NP as subject and the participle as predicate. Drawing on Myler’s (2016) analysis of have and insights from the literature on stative passives and the internal structure of participles, we show that the participles in these constructions may denote event and state tokens, and that different semantic readings of the construction correspond to a single syntactic structure. On the basis of this analysis, we develop a new account of the rise of analytic perfect tenses in Romance. We argue that the trigger for reanalysis was an independent change in the nominal domain — the emergence of a D-layer and in particular the grammaticalization of definite articles — which forced reanalysis specifically in contexts involving inalienably possessed direct objects. Once established in this critical context, the construction spread to new environments, including, for the first time, intransitive verbs.

records.title: Formal Properties of Language as Constraints on Neural Dynamics
keywords: language; syntax; neural dynamics; hopf algebra; meld
records.abstract: What must a neural system be capable of to implement language? Current research annotates stimuli with linguistic variables and tests which electrodes, voxels, or language-model layers predict neural activity. Yet predictive success leaves neural mechanisms under-constrained, and candidate composition rules may fail to preserve distinctions natural language requires. Here, we show that algebraic properties of language can constrain this search space by specifying invariants that candidate mechanisms must preserve, such as non-associative hierarchical grouping, binding that ignores the order of its parts, recursive closure, access to substructures, semantic role compatibility, and transitions through structured workspaces. This constraint-led approach is termed the Neural Admissibility Program (NAP). To illustrate it, syntactic structure building is analyzed algebraically and candidate mechanisms are proposed for each requirement: content-addressable workspace memory (e.g., expander Hopfield networks), graph-structured transient dynamics for scheduling structure-building operations (e.g., stable heteroclinic channels), and a phase-coupled sealing operation that records grouping. Simulations then show that a corrected form of the Marcolli–Berwick entropy-optimized binding gate preserves grouping only within a narrow band of commitment. As an alternative, we propose a novel neural binding operation we term ‘Meld’: two constituent populations converge through shared synapses, integrate sublinearly, and saturate. Meld is, to our knowledge, the closest neurally plausible composition law to the syntactic Merge computation. It preserves every invariant the NAP demands, is built from operations cortex is known to perform, and recovers hierarchical structure at every depth and temperature tested, decoding bracketing to within a few points of the best-performing rival law (ordered role-filler) while remaining order-blind. It predicts that the effective dimensionality of population activity separates alternative bracketings and that the composite depends on how far its constituents disagree. Importantly, the laws that decode bracketing most accurately are a priori inadmissible, indicating that neural decoding accuracy alone cannot adjudicate between mechanisms. By specifying how neural dynamics can remain faithful to linguistic structure, the NAP changes the criterion by which neural implementations of cognition are evaluated.

records.title: Towards a typology of pseudo antipassives: an Austronesian perspective
records.abstract: Although the Austronesian family is widely regarded as a hotspot for antipassive constructions, a closer investigation of 53 languages from Taiwan and Maritime Southeast Asia challenges this view. Philippine-type Austronesian languages have often been analyzed as exhibiting an alternation between a basic transitive construction and a corresponding antipassive. Yet when established typological criteria are applied consistently to the constructions commonly referred to as Actor Voice, genuine antipassives prove to be rare in western Austronesian. We further demonstrate how these putative antipassives form a continuum of semitransitives, characterized by a general decrease in semantic transitivity while often still featuring a patient that retains various traits of a core argument. Not only does this cline enhance our understanding of how antipassive-like constructions may develop over time, but it also suggests that syntactic intransitivity is not necessarily the endpoint of discourse-driven changes that reduce clausal transitivity. Moreover, it undermines the prevalent ergative view of western Austronesian languages and lends new support to accusative and symmetrical voice analyses, both maintaining that Austronesian-style voice does not alter clausal transitivity. The Austronesian pseudo antipassives thus underscore the importance of approaching typological classifications with caution and situating language-specific analyses within the broader typological literature.

records.title: The Haft and the Eye: Being, Representation, and the AI Epoch
records.abstract: This version introduces the devil child from Golding's final chapter as the subject of Tuami's carving, names the unspeakable remainder for the first time in this paper, and points to the companion papers for its full development. Closes with the claim that what the haft carries is what the representational project will spend the rest of its history trying to return to. The structural and linguistic dimensions of this argument are developed in the companion papers already available on this server: "Pictures and Figures: Golding, Halliday, and the Stratum Closest to Being" grounds the claim in Halliday's Systemic Functional Grammar and Golding's narrative enactment of pre-representational consciousness; "The Sail and the Wind: Why Proximity Is Not Access" develops the empirical case through gerontolinguistic research on aging and developmental research on dreaming. Readers encountering the trilogy for the first time may find it useful to begin with either companion paper before returning to the more abstract philosophical argument made here. This paper is the first of three companion papers developing the connected argument about Being, representation, and the conditions under which human beings can access the pre-representational ground of experience. The argument begins here with the philosophical and epochal case: tracing an arc from pre-Socratic immediacy through Cartesian modernity to artificial intelligence, the paper argues that AI represents the completion of the Western representational project — the first technology to externalize not the products of human cognition but the generative loop itself, without embodied ground behind it.

records.title: Thai Tough-Constructions and the Tough Signature
records.abstract: We investigate the tough-construction in Thai, focusing on two exceptional properties. First, Thai tough-constructions may involve a potentially unconstrained dependency, and second, the gap in the embedded clause can be in the subject position. While these facts superficially support a heterogeneous view of tough-constructions across the world’s languages, on closer inspection, we come to a different conclusion. We argue that unconstrained dependencies and subject gaps are not a function of Thai tough-constructions, but instead reflect the fact that Thai has an undiagnosed broad subject position. Once controlled for, Thai tough-constructions look surprisingly like other well-documented cases. Ultimately, we are concerned not with variation in tough-constructions, but rather crosslinguistic similarities.

records.title: 3-on-3 restrictions and PCC typology: a reply to Pancheva and Zubizaretta (2018)
records.abstract: Restrictions on clitic combinations are generally in place when a ditransitive is expressed with both direct object and indirect object clitics. The best-studied such restrictions involve local persons, as in classic person-case constraint (PCC) effects—e.g., in French, banning combinations of local person DO clitics with IO clitics (strong PCC). Many languages also impose restrictions on combinations of 3rd person clitics (*3-on-3). Spanish, for instance, bans combinations of 3rd dative + 3rd accusative, requiring the dative to be replaced by the so-called “spurious se” (Perlmutter 1971). These two types of restrictions have typically been attributed to separate grammatical rules, if not entirely separate components of the grammar. However, in recent work, Pancheva and Zubizarreta (2018) have proposed a partial unification of *3-on-3 and classic PCC, treating both as grounded in syntactic licensing principles. This theory predicts a typological interaction: 3-on- 3 restrictions will be found only in certain languages that also constrain combinations including local persons. In this paper, I argue that this prediction is false. In Ubykh (NW Caucasian), no restriction is imposed on clitic combinations involving local persons--there is no PCC effect of any type--but 3-on-3 combinations show clitic opacity effects reminiscent of spurious se. Capturing this pattern requires grammatical rules for the 3-on-3 context that are not grounded in PCC syntax, thus making a case for the independence of the two types of ditransitive person restrictions more generally.

records.title: “ERGATIVITY, properly aligned” – And the case of SHIPIBO
records.abstract: Common sense is prone to error, especially when it comes to scientific matters. “Ergativity” is a concept fraught with bias. Not every language that appears to be ergative actually is one. SHIPIBO is a very good example. It is a DIFFERENTIALLY-marked-subject/argument language, mistakenly considered to be ergative. This SQUIB is the answer to reviews of "Ergativity, properly aligned". [typo-reduced version v.1.3]

records.title: Syntax and Semantics of Old Iranian Relative Clauses: Theoretical and Formal Implications
records.abstract: Old Iranian languages display patterns of relativization that do not fit neatly into existing accounts. This thesis examines free relatives and correlatives, primarily in Old Avestan, with comparative evidence from Old Persian and Young Avestan. Its first chapter addresses a basic methodological problem: how can we reliably classify constructions in ancient and low-resource languages when interpretations are uncertain and native-speaker judgments unavailable? It develops a replicable algorithm that moves from formal schema induction to typological comparison and the testing of structural and interpretive predictions. Using this method, the Old Avestan data are situated within the cross-linguistic typology of headless and head-internal free relatives, correlatives, and related constructions. The comparison establishes these patterns as grammatical constructions in their own right, rather than variants of postnominal relative clauses, and motivates expanding the cross-linguistics typology of free relatives to include non-interrogative-based forms. The thesis also proposes a novel analysis of free relatives at the syntax-semantics interface. Its central advantage is that it derives the maximalizing semantics of free relatives without recourse to empty categories or silent operators. It further examines Old Avestan generalizing relative clauses and relates their generalizing expressions to Negative Polarity and Free Choice Items. The surveys of Old Persian and Young Avestan show that these constructions are less productive and less varied outside Old Avestan.

records.title: A Note on the Apparent Polarity Status of English Bare Much
keywords: polarity negation much many few little
records.abstract: The apparent negative polarity behavior seen with 'much' and 'many' is a side effect of a licensing requirement holding of the silent AMOUNT or NUMBER that they cooccur with, much as in Kayne (2021) on 'long'. The overall conclusion is that negative polarity is not a primitive of the language faculty, at least not in the kind of cases discussed. Silent elements and their licensing requirements are more fundamental.

records.title: The Nanosyntax of the Adjective. Evidence from Czech
records.abstract: This book follows up on the seminal work by Bobaljik, who proposed a containment relation among the positive, comparative and superlative degrees. The starting point of our work was the observation that some languages provide a much richer morphology: we discovered cases where the comparative is derived from the positive by the addition of two or even three independent suffixes, while in other cases the comparative is not derived from the positive, but from a shorter, truncated form of the positive. We argue that the full morphological complexity can be derived by unifying the original claim that the superlative syntactically contains the comparative, and the comparative syntactically contains the positive with a more fine-grained decomposition, using the ingredients familiar from the semantics research distinguishing scales, standards of comparison, measure phrases, etc. Specifically, we argue for a syntactic representation consisting of two scales, with the comparative showing both scales and the positive only one, along the lines of Kennedy and Levin’s 2008 work. Each scale is in turn represented syntactically by the same four features of standard of comparison, dimension of the scale (e.g., size or speed), direction of the scale (positive vs. negative, as in fast vs. slow) and perhaps a measure phrase (which we call ‘distance’). We show that this combination yields exactly the rich morpho-syntactic patterns observed.

records.title: Chinese Dialectal Parameterisation and Microvariation: From Hong Kong to the World
records.abstract: As a child growing up in a triglossic society such as Hong Kong, my native intuitions in Chinese are shared between standard literary Mandarin and the Cantonese vernacular, which has proven to be useful to my research in comparative parametric syntax and teaching Chinese as a foreign language. Applying formal parameters based on universal cartography, the main dialectal differences between Cantonese and Mandarin can be classified in three types: 1) functional categories with different selectional properties 2) different word order of the same lexical items 3) syntactic operations that occur in certain dialects but not in others. This paper provides an outline of how my triglossic upbringing laid the foundation for my current work in linguistic research and language teaching.

records.title: Linguistmaster, a Taskmaster-inspired game
records.abstract: "Taskmaster" is a British game show where contestants attempt to complete a series of challenges. "Syntaxmaster" is a linguistic version of one of the tasks from S12E4 [ https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=b_oXhJqhVB0 ]. Ultimately, the goal of the game is to decipher a message. But this is just a pretext to get students to retrieve important syntactic concepts. The deciphering is done by pairing linguistic concepts or definitions with data that illustrate them. Each concept is assigned to a symbol, while each data point is assigned a letter. By pairing each concept with the data that exemplifies it, the players arrive at a cipher that decodes the message. For example, let's say that the message to be decoded contains the symbol "♠." This symbol is associated with the following definition: "An anaphor must be c-commanded by its antecedent." In order to figure out which letter "♠" corresponds to, the players must inspect a set of sentences and converge on a pair of sentences like "Mary praised herself" vs. "*Mary's grandparents praised herself." Assuming further that these data are associated with the letter "S," players will, then, have uncovered part of the cipher, so that they are now able to translate the "♠" symbol in the coded message into an "S." The game is highly adaptable. The instructor can create their own "[insert subfield]master." The questions/concepts and the data can be changed too, so the level of the difficulty can be easily modulated. The message and cipher, needless to say, can be changed as well. Click on "PDF" to download an instantiation of the game, implemented as "Syntaxmaster." .tex versions of these files, but with minimal formatting, so that you can easily create your own version, can be downloaded here: [ https://www.overleaf.com/read/rhjtpdyqfcpr#3abd32 ]. Second version (2026 09 14): some typos corrected.

records.title: On abstinence and avoidance
records.abstract: In this paper, I inspect two types of readings that emerge in a range of environments, such as in negative imperatives, under 'not want', under 'fear', etc.: (i) ABSTAIN readings, which convey willingness to prevent someone from intentionally engaging in some kind of act, and (ii) AVOID readings, which convey willingness to prevent a potentially unintended outcome. The ABSTAIN vs. AVOID distinction has a variety of grammatical reflexes cross-linguistically, e.g., anti-/re-licensing of 'some'-indefinites in English: 'Don't call anyone!' (which asks the addressee to abstain from intentionally engaging in the activity of calling some person or other) vs. 'Don't (accidentally) call someone!' (which cautions the addressee against accidentally calling some person or other). I will focus on perfective vs. imperfective aspect and distribution of indefinites in Russian. I will argue that the relevant complements in ABSTAIN vs. AVOID cases have distinct compositional structures: there is a situation layer in AVOID, but not in ABSTAIN cases. This will allow us to explain the relevant Russian facts about aspect and indefinites, but will also establish a framework for building accounts of grammatical reflexes of the ABSTAIN vs. AVOID distinction cross-linguistically. The choice between the two compositional structures in the environments at hand is then driven by global pragmatic considerations about preventing unwanted scenarios, yielding the diverging inferences about intentional vs. accidental actions arising in the two cases.

records.title: Multilingual development: English in a global context, by Peter Siemund (book review)
records.abstract: The way that the author has framed the problem of multilingualism has presented us with a dilemma. Just as during an earlier expansion of scholarship and learning – when East Asia and Europe each needed their lingua franca – today’s global imperative for a language of international communication has selected English. At the same time as English-language venues have become the indispensable tool of research and cross-cultural discussion in almost every discipline, they have also suffered the effects of an impending corruption, particularly in academia. More than for any other major or cross-national language, publication in English, in print and online, has become the favoured channel for propagating a new genre of pseudo-science and anti-scientific critique of the advances of the Enlightenment. Depending on the prospects for greater plurality, a shift towards a new international linguistic multi-polarity may not be as impractical as it once appeared to be. Journal of Multilingual and Multicultural Development (2026) 47, 3: 1950-1952.

records.title: Variable-flavor attitude reports without underspecification
records.abstract: We examine an apparent case of a variable-flavor attitude predicate, the verb kä in Äiwoo, which can receive ‘think’, ‘say’, or ‘want’ translations. We argue that this verb denotes linguistic production, which may be mental or physical (thus capturing its use in doxastic and assertive reports). Its use for bouletic reports arises from combining it with an overt priority modal (the prefix nä-) in the embedded clause, whose semantic contribution can be independently established from its use in unembedded contexts.

records.title: Concatenation, $-theory, and Phonosyntax
records.abstract: [This is part of a larger project to build a formal grammar of Japanese.] I propose phonosyntax as part of the phonological component, in which phonological strings are recursively merged to build the input for prosody. The proposal is motivated by merge-sensitive phonological processes, including a recursive accent rule and an opaque segmental process, and by a preceding theory of semantics. I put forth formal definitions of two phonological processes that exemplify this merge-based subcomponent of phonology, namely, concatenation and $-propagation. The former accounts for joining of two phonological strings, a phenomenon found in virtually all languages. The latter accounts for stress assignment of Tokyo Japanese. As a consequence of these proposals, I suggest from both phonological and semantic perspectives that some aspects of what has been called syntax may be better understood as part of phonology.

records.title: The semantics of profane quasi-verbs: Social relations in a dynamic framework
records.abstract: Though profane imprecations like F*** you! have received no attention in formal semantics, we might expect our theory of linguistic meaning to have something to say about such common expressions. In this paper, I discuss the nature of the meanings of profane quasi-verbs (Quang 1971) that function syntactically like f*** in the example above, and I provide a formal model that can account for some important aspects of their meaning and conversational use. This analysis throws light on the role of social relations in semantics and pragmatics.

records.title: The landscape of negative biases: modality, exclamative-questions and exclamatives
records.abstract: The interaction between modality and evidentiality has received considerable attention, but much less is known about the interaction between modality and speech-act operators. This paper argues that this interface is crucial to understanding how evaluative meanings arise with epistemic modals, particularly in non-information-seeking interrogatives and exclamatives. We develop an account of modal bias as a manipulable component of modal meaning and propose that question and exclamative operators can themselves act as bias manipulators. The empirical domain is Italian epistemic future, whose exceptional flexibility makes visible the mechanisms underlying this interaction. Building on previous work, we analyze the \textbf{Italian future} as a universal epistemic modal with no default bias, rather than as an evidential or a marker of subjective credence. Its flexibility derives from a metaevaluative layer at which the speaker’s evaluation of the prejacent is encoded and can be modified. The analysis distinguishes two mechanisms of negative bias: in `mica' future questions, bias emerges through the interaction of modality, QUES and the particle; in future exclamatives, it is introduced directly by EXCL. More generally, the paper argues that speech-act operators participate in semantic composition with modal meaning by manipulating its metaevaluative dimension, while remaining distinct from modality itself.

records.title: Interpreting Clausal Movement
records.abstract: In this paper we provide both support for, and a challenge to, Takahashi's (2010) proposal that a moved clausal complement must involve a DP structure headed by a covert determiner. Based on data from Georgian, we show that (i) bare CPs cannot move to the left—topicalization in the language is restricted to DPs, just like in English; (ii) CPs can move to the right, and in fact must do so when they are not encapsulated in the DP structure. We argue that rightwards extraposition of CPs is semantically vacuous and driven purely by a constraint on linearization: Georgian CPs are head-initial, while VPs are head-final, and thus remaining in situ would lead to the violation of the Final-Over-Final Constraint (FOFC) (Biberauer et al. 2009a,b, Biberauer and Sheehan 2012, a.o.). For this reason, Georgian bare CPs must vacuously move to conform to the FOFC. We discuss the implications of this conclusion for the ban on bare CP movement leftwards.

records.title: Perception of Difficulty Changes in Sign Language: The Influence of Middle School Students' Sign Language Cognition and Basic Linguistic Knowledge
records.abstract: This study examines changes in secondary school students' perception of the difficulty of Chinese Sign Language (CSL), and analyzes the suggestions proposed by participants. Through a questionnaire survey, data on sign language awareness were collected from 184 secondary school students. The results indicate that although most students had been exposed to sign language through online platforms, public welfare activities, and other channels, their perception of its difficulty shifted noticeably after exposure to basic sign language linguistics. Notably, students commonly reported that their unfamiliarity with sign language stemmed primarily from a lack of formal learning platforms.

records.title: Multiple Pluralization Strategies in Akan: A Split Number Approach
records.abstract: Recent work on number has shown that number features may be distributed across different layers of nominal structure. Akan provides a revealing case: multiple number morphemes can occur within a single nominal and differ in their distribution and interpretation. This paper argues that these patterns reflect a split nominal architecture in which number is distributed across three functional heads: a low nominalizing head, a higher renominalizing head associated with humanness, and a Num head. Each plural morpheme realizes a distinct structural position and may make a different semantic contribution. The analysis provides new evidence for split number in Niger-Congo languages.
